items.title: Moto and Mountain Bike Icon Öhlins Debuts a Lust-Worthy Gravel Fork
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The GXF30 M.1 from the Swedish suspension brand offers clean functionality and bold aesthetics to the gravel market.
items.lbText:
The legendary auto and mountain bike suspension brand Öhlins has entered the gravel suspension market with the GXF30 M.1 short-travel fork. Öhlins has been heavily involved in mountain bikes in recent years, with particular success in downhill racing, making the pivot to gravel feel like a natural progression.

Nevertheless, the brand is coming into the market well after the other big suspension brands entered the gravel market.

Despite the crowded market, Öhlins is still leaning into its standing as one of the most well-respected suspension brands with a simple yet refined gravel option that is a direct competitor to the Fox TC 32 and the RockShox Rudy. No remote lockout, no stripped-down inverted design, just 40mm of travel delivered in a clean, highly aesthetic design.

“We are not the first suspension company entering the gravel segment, but we wanted to do it with our own philosophy. For more than 50 years, Öhlins has been dedicated to off-road racing, and we firmly believe that every off-road discipline benefits from suspension. Gravel is not an exception.

“Our objective was simple: improve rider comfort, increase grip on technical terrain, and provide greater confidence and safety on every ride. These three principles guided every engineering decision throughout the development process. The result is a suspension fork that allows riders to go faster while feeling more in control.”

When it comes to gravel suspension, there seem to be two camps. On one side are forks that are essentially smaller versions of mountain bike forks. On the other side are forks that are trying to achieve gravel suspension through unique means.

Öhlins follows the former model, building a size-down version of a mountain bike fork instead of coming in with any revolutionary ideas. It doesn’t rock the boat; instead, the GXF30 M.1 is built to be a rock-solid 40mm fork that is best suited for small bump control and traction management.

It is worth noting that the GXF30 M.1 is only offered in that 40mm travel, compared to the RockShox Rudy or the Fox TC 32 which have multiple travel options. That was the travel that the brand felt met its riding objectives without changing the geometry and fit of suspension-corrected geometry. Additionally, changing the travel would require replacing the fork’s piston rod assembly, which further cemented the plan for Öhlins to restrict the travel to 40mm.

The GXF30 M.1 does, however, have a highly adjustable crown-based lockout. Beyond just a binary lock/unlock setting, the GXF30 M.1 offers more interstitial settings to control how stiff the fork is. Adjustability is a tricky point for gravel forks, historically, especially around lockout settings. With the simple design, adjustability seems to be a big priority for Öhlins.

In terms of the fork’s construction, Öhlins has opted for 30mm stanchions—the same diameter as the Rudy—and the brand’s FTX14 damper. Dampers have been an area where gravel suspension has been split. With the gravel use case, forks can get away with limited or no damper, but it still can improve the overall feel of the fork, especially at high speeds over rough terrain.

Öhlins has zeroed in on the damper construction and the unique demands of a damper on short-travel gravel forks, as an area where its expertise in a wide variety of high-end racing suspension can make a difference.

The downside of any robust suspension damper is weight. The Öhlins GXF30 M.1 is no different, with the system weighing in at a claimed 1,249 grams. That said, that weight is still around 100 grams less than the RockShox Rudy and in line with the Fox TC 32, so Öhlins has managed to minimize the weight penalty.

The Öhlins GXF30 M.1 is available now, but in a limited run of just 300 launch edition units. The limited availability is in line with the brand’s positioning of the GXF 30M.1 as a true premium gravel fork.

Accordingly, the fork is on the more expensive side at an MSRP of $995 USD and €895 EUR. Nevertheless, at that price, the classic Öhlins Racing Yellow paint scheme is standard in launch-edition forks and does give the fork a striking yet classic look.

To learn more about the ins and outs of the GXF30 M.1, visit Öhlins’ website .

items.title: The reasons behind Ferrari's US GP upgrades
Yankees Mailbag: A qualifying offer conundrum
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
Good afternoon everyone, it’s time to dive back into the mailbag and answer some of your questions. Remember to send in your questions for our bi-weekly call by e-mail to pinstripealleyblog [at] gmail [dot] com.

It would seem a qualifying offer to Bednar is a given. The QO to Jazz also seems likely as Yankees will perceive he will reject it and, unlike the gamble with Grisham that was a huge miscalculation on Cashman’s part, Jazz will probably reject it. Your thoughts?

I don’t know if I’d agree with your second point, as reports have come out saying that the team is actually unlikely to offer the qualifying offer to Jazz Chisholm Jr. this offseason. The gamble over whether Chisholm would accept the deal or not mirroring what happened with Trent Grisham last year is probably informing their decision on that matter, as while I wouldn’t hate bringing Jazz back on a one-year deal the team seems to be angling towards allowing him to walk. Whereas Grisham was coming off of a career-best year, Chisholm had his worst season in pinstripes, but the argument could be made that Grisham knew the market was a lot more crowded with excellent choices while Chisholm is still one of the best options in a free agent field lacking a true superstar or even many stars to compete against.

With that in mind, it might be a more reasonable gamble to give Chisholm the QO and not lose him for nothing than it was with Grisham, but again the team clearly cares about their budget and potentially handing out over $45 million in 2027 salary between Bednar and Chisholm before free agency even opens might restrict them too much to make other moves. I’m not thrilled with the backup option to Chisholm being running Anthony Volpe at the keystone, but if it leads to improvements elsewhere on the roster I could see the logic in the move — and we’ll talk about where that upgrade is most needed in a moment. Ultimately, while I know Chisholm had a disappointing year for New York (and perhaps set himself up to with talk of having a 50-50 season during spring), I think it’s unlikely they field a better player at his position than him in 2027 and I think that makes the QO a worthwhile choice, but it looks like that won’t be the case.

With Ryan McMahon struggling to solve the Yankees’ third base problem as hoped, do you think the team will try to trade him this offseason, or is a DFA more likely? Given his $16 million salary for 2027, what teams, if any, could make a compelling case for acquiring him despite the financial commitment?

Now, here is where the resources need to be allocated to improve the position. Third base has been a black hole for damn near a decade at this point, with only small bursts of quality play like Gio Urshela’s 2019 run sparkling before being swallowed back up by the void. Ryan McMahon was never expected to be a quality hitter when the Yankees acquired him, but they were certainly expecting better than the 78 wRC+ he posted in 124 games. He was also expected to overcome his offensive capabilities by providing stellar defense, and while he lived up to that in 2025 his play at the hot corner sizzled out completely in 2026 leading to a frustrating experience where he really didn’t provide much of anything.

That’s not really a compelling case to bring towards any potential suitors, so while the team would surely love to trade him away for whatever they could get, it would require tacking on prospects to get even partial salary relief at the moment. Normally I’d say they’re better off just going the DFA route like they did with DJ LeMahieu and Aaron Hicks, but the team is also staring down the prospect of moving on from Giancarlo Stanton’s contract as well and I’m not sure that Hal Steinbrenner could stomach two deadweight contracts for players not even on the team anymore. Of the two, it would be easier to sell McMahon with a prospect attached than it would Stanton, who has a full no-trade clause and an extra year on his deal even if it is a team option. If push comes to shove the team is better off moving on from McMahon and DFA’ing him would suffice, but if they can find an angle to move him that doesn’t cost any of their blue chip prospects it wouldn’t be a bad move to make — they can’t all make it to the big leagues, and using prospect capital to improve the roster by subtraction is still an improvement. I trust the player development team to find enough talent to keep the pipeline greased up, and they didn’t offload too much in this year’s deadline.

Assuming no additions during free agency, who would be the best leadoff hitter? Rice and Judge needs to be 2-4. Lombard, Bellinger, or Volpe could be options. Wells, García, Stanton, and Jones makes no sense.

If you’re forcing me to keep Ben Rice and Aaron Judge somewhere in the 2-4 range then I’d set my sights on George Lombard Jr. earning the leadoff role, as the rookie showed solid results at the plate during his whirlwind debut in the second half and throughout the postseason. The defensive misplays were atypical of his performance down in the minors, but the bat showed some promise and the only other candidate I see would be Volpe, who has already had his chance to be a leadoff hitter to no avail. However, what I would rather do in this scenario is just have Rice hit leadoff, bat Judge second and have Bellinger flanking him with Lombard or Jones at cleanup and García hitting fifth. Rice proved that he’s a capable enough table-setter, and without an ideal OBP-driven player in the lineup as is you might as well give your best hitters the earliest chances to get up to bat.

However, what I would rather do in this scenario is just have Rice hit leadoff, bat Judge second and have Bellinger flanking him with Lombard or Jones at cleanup and García hitting fifth. Rice proved that he’s a capable enough table-setter, and without an ideal OBP-driven player in the lineup as is you might as well give your best hitters the earliest chances to get up to bat.

items.title: Change captain? Play the kids? How to solve the problems at Manchester United
items.author: Jamie Jackson
items.content:
The beleaguered Michael Carrick’s job is on the line, but there are steps he can take to revive the stricken club

The big question as Bournemouth arrive for Sunday’s 2pm kick-off at Old Trafford is whether Michael Carrick will show his authority by stripping the captaincy from Bruno Fernandes and/or dropping Manchester United’s five-times player of the year. On Friday, Carrick refused to deny he may do so, but the bigger picture concerns whether cashing in on the Portuguese and his fellow mutineer, Lisandro Martínez, in the winter window would be prescient to initiate a new era. Fernandes and Martínez are out of contract in the close season (the club has an extra year’s option in both cases) and, judging by recent behaviour, intend to leave. So yielding, say, £40m and £25m respectively for them in January would allow investment as the rebuild begins. Even a few days on, Fernandes’s words in Como seem incredible: “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” he said after Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation. Fernandes’s open questioning of the tactics is a challenge to the head coach’s authority and we wait to see how/if Carrick will face it down. If Carrick acts and proves he is not a lame duck then even if he is removed a favour is done for his successor.

items.title: Anti-Pogačar Tour? ‘We Want to Keep the Suspense,’ Says Prudhomme
items.author: ahood
items.content: Tour de France boss Prudhomme denies the 2027 route targets Pogačar, saying more TT kilometers could keep the yellow jersey fight alive.
items.lbText:
Prudhomme denied the Tour de France course is designed against Pogačar. (Photo: Getty Images)

Is the 2027 Tour de France route designed to make life hard for Tadej Pogačar ?

No way, says Tour boss Christian Prudhomme .

The Tour de France created a stir Thursday with its 2027 course reveal in what’s a radical departure from the past several editions .

Instead of endless uphill kickers and non-stop climbing that seemed like a red carpet for King Pog, the 114th edition is packed with two individual time trials and features only three major mountaintop finales.

Fan reaction was quick: This is an anti-Pogačar course .

Prudhomme pushed back, but didn’t hide the fact that this year’s design is far from ideal from the Slovenian superstar.

“We’ll never design a course for just one rider. Instead, we design courses for different types of riders,” Prudhomme told RMC Radio .

“We’ve done it for puncheurs for years because it’s more exciting to watch and less dangerous than a classic sprint finish. Now, we’re adding more time trials because we want to rebalance things.”

Prudhomme and the ASO braintrust are about to find out.

Two individual time trials totaling 71 kilometers, the most in 15 years, give Remco Evenepoel and rising French star Paul Seixas a chance to counter the Slovenian’s mountain firepower.

After watching Pogačar dominate the Tour since 2024 and perhaps listening to murmurs that the Slovenian’s dominance is becoming boring, the Tour race director wanted to change things up.

With the most individual time trial kilometers since Bradley Wiggins won in 2012, Tour officials are giving Evenepoel room to put his biggest advantage to work.

Rising French star Seixas also gets terrain to challenge the established order — if he decides to race the Tour.

“We have a rider who has dominated the time trial for years, Remco Evenepoel. There’s also Paul Seixas, who is very good in this discipline,” Prudhomme said. “This could be a way to rebalance the time lost in the mountains.”

Prudhomme’s explanation, though, gets to the heart of the challenge facing anyone trying to build suspense around cycling’s most dominant rider.

From the monuments to the grand tours, Pogačar has been all but unbeatable since 2024. Only a mid-race crash that ended his season cost him a likely Vuelta a España crown.

After several Tour editions of ever-increasingly difficult courses, ASO thought it was time for a change.

The start in the UK with three stages means that there won’t be a major mountain summit until the end of the first full week.

The rise of Evenepoel against the clock and Seixas’ growing all-around abilities means, that at least in the eyes of course designers, having more TT’s now makes more sense.

In earlier editions, course designers saw how Pogačar was crushing rivals both in time trials and in the mountains. Jonas Vingegaard stopped him in his tracks for two years.

“For time trials, when the same riders gain time in the mountains and in the time trial, there’s no incentive to increase the time for the individual time trials since the result is the same,” Prudhomme said.

So in that context, Prudhommme and Co. came up with a 2027 course that’s a bit of an old-school throwback.

Sprinters see more chances, including a day-one shot at yellow, and the time trial is back in vogue.

A flat 38km test through Loire château country in the first week should suit the pure specialists. The second TT just before the Pyrénées is on a 33km loop around Toulouse that features a short but steep “wall” with about 10km to go.

On paper, that could favor Evenepoel and perhaps even Seixas, whose TT chops are improving. He finished third to an unstoppable Belgian “aero-rocket” at the Montréal time trial worlds.

“It’s a clash of styles between time trial specialists who gain time in the time trial and climbers who gain time in the mountains and lose it in the time trial,” he said.

Prudhomme called the Col du Portet the Tour’s “new Tourmalet” and said the final mountain stages in the Pyrénées will prove decisive.

“This could turn the tables 48 hours before the final arrival in Paris,” he said. “We want to keep the suspense going for as long as possible.”

But will the Tour makeover work and keep the tension in the race all the way to the final weekend?

“It’s not an anti-Pogačar strategy,” Prudhomme told RMC Radio . “Pogačar loves challenges. So, he might be the one to win both time trials.”

So much for finding a chink in the Slovenian’s armor.

items.title: How open is that championship window?
items.author: Joshua Diemert
items.content:
Everything in the world is different than it was in 2016 — sometimes I am paid to say the obvious. Ten years ago we saw multiple curses end, billy goats and black cats forever exorcised, as Kris Bryant threw to Anthony Rizzo and the Cubs had finally won it all. Bryant was the MVP of the National League that year, a seven and a half win season in his sophomore campaign. Anthony Rizzo was just 26 and finished fourth in that MVP race, Addison Russell was 22 manning shortstop and he also received votes for the league’s top individual honor.

That Cubs team is known for their collection of home grown bats, but the pitching staff was talented in its own right, albeit a little more mercenary. Jake Arrieta wasn’t quite the Cy Young winner he was the year before but the Cubs had four three-win starters in their rotation, and while Kyle Hendricks was the only one under the age of 30, the combination of a very good rotation, elite homegrown (read: cheap) position players, and a big market with the capacity to spend…surely the North Side would see more than one pennant from that group.

Ten years on the Cubs did make the playoffs five times, with two division titles, but that’s mostly it. Anthony Rizzo’s career effectively ended when Fernando Tatis Jr.‘s hip slammed into his head, Kris Bryant has become one of the great baseball tragedies of our era, and Russell abused his wife and is playing in the Mexican League. The Cubs are a playoff team again, and flags fly forever — especially ones tied to 108 year old poles — but you kind of have to think that proto-dynasty left something on the table.

A year later, the Yankees themselves seemed on the edge of a dynasty. Aaron Judge should have been MVP, Luis Severino was one of the three best pitchers in the AL, Greg Bird wasn’t just locking down first base, he was creating playoff memories, and Gary Sánchez seemed to be a foundational piece of a winning team for a decade to come. That decade’s nearly come and gone, Aaron Judge has lived up to that potential, but as for the rest of what seemed like an ascendant group…let’s put it this way, Sánchez might well win a World Series before Judge does.

The Yankees haven’t had a losing season in my lifetime. The seasons when they do miss the playoffs stand out like scars, for the entire time I’ve been aware of the concept of baseball, the team’s pretty much been in the so-called window of contention. They could have won the World Series this year, they could have last year, could have the year before, and on and on.

The Red Sox got their ring, like the Cubs, before doing the unthinkable and dealing away one of the best players in franchise history over money. They’ve remained a playoff team, even knocking the Yankees out of the postseason in the so-called Baby Bombers era.

The World Series starts tonight, with two teams built on the cheap, that came out of their respective leagues as the top seeds. The Brewers have been in the so-called championship window for two seasons now, the Rays seem to enter and swiftly exist theirs nearly year to year. The Cubs and Red Sox had to learn sometimes you only get one, no matter how sustainable things look. The Yankees haven’t even gotten one, and stare down an uncertain 2027 with an aging roster.

The window’s never as open as you think it is. Gotta climb through now.

items.title: 'I will retire soon' – Marlen Reusser discusses future as she gives thumbs up to Paula Blasi's arrival at Movistar in 2027
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Marlen Reusser has given her strongest hint yet that her racing days may soon be numbered when the Swiss time trialling star was asked at the Tour de France Femmes presentation about the imminent arrival of Spanish up-and-coming racer Paula Blasi at her Movistar squad.

Blasi had a breakthrough season in 2026 while racing for UAE Team L'IMAD, winning La Vuelta Femenina and Amstel Gold Race, before taking fifth at her debut Tour de France Femmes.

Reusser also had a highly successful Tour, winning the mid-race TT and holding the lead for three days before losing the yellow jersey on Mont Ventoux, before dropping to 14th overall after crashing on the final day in Nice.

Speaking at the Tour de France Femmes route presentation, Reusser also said that it was a pity there was no individual time trial in 2027 but praised the inclusion of the team time trial on stage 3 in London and the Ardennes-like stages 2 and 8.

Whilst pointing out that the Tour is often decided, at least in part, on less mountainous stages, she also said that she was confident of her chances of handling the critical Puy de Dôme climb and its ultra-steep finale.

"I think the Puy de Dôme is closed off to riders right now" – the road is usually shut because the entire volcano is an ecologically sensitive site – "but I remember watching the Tour go up it in 2023; it's a cool climb to finish the Tour," Reusser said.

"I think I can manage the slopes [of 12%] well. I have no idea if it's possible to recon, but if so I'll do it."

Regarding the absence of an individual time trial, reigning world and European champion Reusser confirmed she would have liked that "because that does something very different with the GC. It's not the same. But in any case I love the discipline [of team time trialling], and I think that's very cool."

The very hilly stages could, in any case, be as important for the GC as the setpiece mountain days, of which there is really only the last, as Reusser pointed out, to the point where they might actually decide the race overall. Stage 4 of last year's Tour was a good example of this, where it played a major part in sorting out the GC, with Pauline Ferrand-Prévot showing significant signs of weakness that day.

"Sometimes it's like this, we look at the big mountain stages, but often these [hilly] stages are actually the more important," Reusser said.

"I was just asked if next year's Tour is not as hard as this year. Ok, the big mountains are there, they sound hard, but these hilly stages are even harder in a way, so they can be very crucial for the GC. We saw it last year."

As for whether there would be another 'Project Dijon' for Reusser, similar to the one she built around the time trial last July in the Tour de France Femmes, Reusser smiled but said it was too early to target specific stages.

"I am sure my DS is waiting in the back there; we'll make plans, we have a lot of time to think about what we're going to do with this race, and we'll have some projects for sure," she said..

The question of how long Reusser will continue racing, though, emerged when she was asked how she felt about the arrival of Blasi on the team. Under contract until the end of 2027, Reusser said that she would retire "soon" and pointed out that at 35, she was no longer as young as she once was.

Reusser also said that having a rider like Blasi on the squad offered Movistar an excellent opportunity to plan for a double assault on the Tour GC, given the Spaniard's proven ability to attack in hilly terrain as she did to win Amstel Gold Race last year.

"For Paula, I think this Tour route is perfect because when you see the Ardennes-like stages, I think it's good to have good riders because you can make good tactics," she reasoned.

"And I think she will want to win the Tour in the future, and I think that's a nice thing. I will retire soon. I'm not the youngest anymore, so I think it makes sense to have her on the team; she's a very big talent. It is the Spanish team, too, so that's nice."

Reusser's career has seen her take multiple top time trial titles, including the World Championships as well as holding the leader's jersey in the Tour last summer.

But if she is now thinking that she may be hanging up her wheels in the shorter rather than the longer term, whilst clearly with plans to shine next summer in the Tour again, then Blasi may well be the ideal way for Movistar to keep battling for Grand Tours in the future.

items.title: Fem van Empel leads Specialized TMRW cyclo-cross team set to 'open new pathways for the next generation' of road talent
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
The Specialized TMRW cycling project is now official, as FDJ United-SUEZ and Specialized confirmed Friday the roster and plans for a new multi-disciplinary approach for a long-term progression to develop talent on the road.

Four core riders will comprise the squad for the 2026-2027 cyclo-cross season, led by three-time cyclo-cross world champion Fem van Empel, who has already provided a sneak preview of the red team kits with her fourth-place finish last weekend at Berencross in Meulebeke, Belgium.

She'll be joined for off-road racing by Anja Grossmann, Amandine Muller and Célia Gery, the trio all U23 riders on the road with FDJ United-SUEZ. Last year, Gery earned the women's U23 bronze medal at Cyclo-cross World Championships in Hulst, while Muller was fifth, both racing for France. Grossman, an 18-year-old talent from Switzerland, went fourth in the women's junior race at CX Worlds last season.

The TMRW brand was created by Tomorrow Group, the owner of FDJ United-SUEZ, to broaden racing into new disciplines. Cyclo-cross was noted as the first step in "strengthening its international presence and nurturing outstanding young talent" as the discipline was seen as a way for riders to develop technical skills and earn racing experience throughout the year.

Stephen Delcourt, the general manager for the Women's WorldTour squad, will serve in the same capacity for the French cyclo-cross team, with Nicolas Maire serving dual roles as well as the sports director.

“What we are building today is rooted in the project developed with FDJ UNITED and SUEZ. Their commitment allows us to look further ahead and prepare for the next stages of our development. Together with Specialized, we share the conviction that giving young athletes the opportunity to grow across disciplines can help them become more complete road riders," Del Court said in a team statement.

"Specialized TMRW brings that ambition to life: to open new pathways for the next generation, explore new sporting opportunities and continue expanding internationally.

"Cyclo-cross has played an important role in the development of some of cycling’s greatest athletes. It provides a demanding environment in which to build technical skills, confidence and racing instinct. We want to give our riders who share that passion the best possible conditions to develop and perform, in full alignment with their goals on the road."

The creation of Specialized TMRW aligns with the road team’s 2030 strategic plan, which management said strived for "excellence in both disciplines".

Van Empel joined FDJ United-SUEZ in mid-September, having taken nearly a year off from racing and securing a release from her multi-year contract with Visma-Lease a Bike. She won a bronze medal in the women's junior road race at European Road Championships in 2023, then impressed the next year on the WorldTour stage with 11th overall at Giro d'Italia and a stage win and points classification title at Tour de l'Avenir Femmes.

Gery, the reigning French elite women's road national champion, won De Brabantse Pijl and a stage at the Giro d'Italia this past season. A dual road and time trial junior champion of Switzerland for two consecutive years, Grossmann impressed at the Road World Championships with fourth in the ITT and a bronze medal in the road race.

Muller, who just turned 20 in mid-October, raced for the AG Insurance Soudal development team the past two seasons, winning the French U23 time trial title twice and the women's elite ITT at the Mediterranean Games.

The Dutch rider's new contract for CX and road goes through 2027, while Gery and Grossman are signed through 2028, Muller through 2029.

"Specialized TMRW builds on the long-term project developed with FDJ UNITED SUEZ, whose commitment remains central to the team’s development," management of the new team said in a statement.

In addition to support from Specialized for the cyclo-cross campaign, the project was also supported by 100%, Shimano and Gobik.

items.title: Why breaking contracts continues to become more common in cycling – Pogačar's agent Carera offers explanation after early exits of Ganna, Carapaz, and Ciccone
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
In previous eras of cycling, a rider breaking their contract early to move teams could have caused major controversy, but in the past few weeks, big-name riders Richard Carapaz, Filippo Ganna, and Giulio Ciccone have all announced exits before the end to join new teams without any obvious hitches.

As riders leaving their current teams early for new pastures becomes more common in the peloton – a practice not just isolated to the men's pros either, with Paula Blasi doing the same – it marks a transformation of the transfer market, with almost any rider available, in theory.

Ciccone's agent Alex Carera, whose agency A&J All Sports also represents Blasi, and a certain Tadej Pogačar, spoke to to explain some of the reasons why this is happening more and more.

"First of all, the average length of contracts has increased - by a lot. Therefore, the likelihood of arguments over a long contract, and even termination, increases," said Carera.

"In essence, if the contract is only two years long and problems arise, you shouldn't wait that long for it to expire, and it's not even worth arguing about. You might sulk for a year, and then you move on. But if, for example, the contract is five years long, it's easy to see that things are very different."

In recent years, several of the biggest riders in the world have reached agreements to leave their teams early: Remco Evenepoel and Primož Roglič both to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, and Juan Ayuso to Lidl-Trek, for example, and Carera says this is down partly to changes in team ownership.

"The second reason is even more crucial, considering that if you want to break an existing contract, you don't just have to negotiate with one team, but also have another team ready to sign you," added Carera.

"Here's the thing: until 5-6 years ago, in most cases the team owners were the team managers, often former cyclists. They didn't have a long-term vision, and they didn't risk potential penalties for signing riders from other teams.

"[Some of the] team owners are... the sponsors themselves. UAE, Decathlon, Lidl, Red Bull, to name a few. They have a more managerial, long-term vision. The cycling team is a key asset for the company, or the fund, unlike before, where there was often no entrepreneurial vision.

"And there's a greater tendency to be more 'aggressive' on the market, because they have to value the annual investment in cycling. Not to mention the fact that the capital invested is much greater. A momentous change."

The UCI overhauled the rules on how riders under contract with one WorldTour can enter into discussions and start the process of joining another. To prevent controversial poaching and the type of polemic that unfolded around the early departure of Cian Uijtdebroeks – another one of Carera's riders – from Visma to Red Bull, the UCI introduced the requirement for a three-party agreement between the rider, their current team, and the new team to enact the move.

Asked what the turning point was for the new types of transfers that were once very rare becoming more and more common by the season, Carera specifically pointed to the transfer of the Belgian, and the financial growth in the sport that followed.

"Cian Uijtdebroeks' early departure from Bora to join Visma in December 2023, a move that generated significant media attention and involved two top teams," he said.

"Until then, early contract terminations occurred once every three years; now, they're about 10 a year. And then, capital has increased enormously: in 2020, if a team had a budget of €25 million, it could be considered wealthy. Now, it would be in the bottom five."

There was one rider whose lengthy ongoing deal is an exception to the new freedom for aggression in the transfer market: Pogačar, whose 2032 contract puts him as one of the most tied-down riders to their ongoing deal, alongside those who have 'lifetime' contracts until retirement: Wout van Aert, Marianne Vos, and Mads Pedersen.

"Is Tadej Pogacar the exception?" asked Ciro Scognamiglio. "Yes, because it has too high a value, the clause is almost symbolic: Tadej has gone beyond the boundaries of cycling," replied Carera.

items.title: Knicks make Dalton Knecht decision involving Kevin McCullar Jr.
items.author: Kento Kato
items.content:
With Karl-Anthony Towns and the New York Knicks’ failed attempt at an extension being public, Miles McBride struggling as he enters a contract year, and Josh Hart and Tyler Kolek also not being extended, fans have speculated on potential roster moves.

And the fans got one today—just not the one most people were necessarily expecting.

On Friday morning, ESPN’s Shams Charania that New York had signed former Tennessee Volunteer and Los Angeles Lakers guard Dalton Knecht to a two-way NBA contract. To make space for the third-year wing, the Knicks are waiving Kevin McCullar Jr.

The Knicks weren’t the only team interested either. On Thursday night, rumors indicated that both the Timberwolves and Raptors were also looking at Knecht.

The former 17th overall pick averaged 9.8PPG and 2.8RPG while shooting 46.1% from the field and 37.6% from three during his rookie season. For spurts, it looked like he could develop into a solid rotation piece for a Lakers team that was still trying to contend with LeBron James at the helm and became a fan favorite after a in the NBA Cup.

Midway through the season, though, Knecht was involved in a trade that would have sent him to the Hornets in exchange for center Mark Williams. After Williams failed his physical and the trade was rescinded, Knecht was forced to return to the Lakers.

Knecht, contrary to belief, finished out the season on a solid note, averaging 8.5PPG while shooting 40.8% from three. Things did take a turn for the worse last season, though. After appearing in 78 games and averaging 19.2MPG in his first season, he averaged just 10.2MPG in just 54 games during the 2025-26 campaign. As many young players do, he struggled with the decreased minutes and inconsistent playing time, leading to a cycle of worse play and even fewer minutes.

The third-year man can still impact the Knicks. He’s just 25 years old and is an above-average shooter with size. In his final year in college, he averaged 21.7PPG on 45.8% shooting from the field and 39.7% shooting from three. It’s not every day you can find that kind of shooting at his height on the waiver wire. But there are plenty of reasons why he saw his minutes dwindle and why he eventually was waived.

Despite being 6’6”, Knecht isn’t much of a defender. He can get lost defensively, and even if he manages to be in the right spots at the right times, he just does not possess the athleticism to be much of a factor on that end. Offensively, he’s shown flashes of being able to utilize his shot to get to other spots on the floor. When a part of the rotation, he was making nice reads off the ball and routinely had nice timely cuts to get easy looks at the rim. But at the end of the day, he’s still best utilized as a spot-up shooter and only a spot-up shooter. He can’t create for himself due to a lack of a reliable handle and certainly doesn’t create for others.

There are also of Knecht not knowing the team’s plays and schemes, which would surely frustrate Mike Brown, who is a very detail- and execution-oriented coach.

Knecht is just 25 years old and has room to grow. If the Knicks, their coaches, and their culture get him right, the shooting and size likely give him more upside than McCullar. But don’t expect him to be a significant contributor. New York likely signed him as a project piece and a deep depth piece. It would take a whole lot for Knecht to not only enter the rotation but to stay there. And in such a circumstance, the Knicks would likely have a lot more than Knecht’s play to worry about.

That being said, it’s still an intriguing low-risk move for a player who may just have needed a change of scenery. It is unfortunate, though, to see McCullar gone given the memorable moments he’s had with this club, regardless of how infrequent they may have been.

On Friday morning, ESPN’s Shams Charania reported that New York had signed former Tennessee Volunteer and Los Angeles Lakers guard Dalton Knecht to a two-way NBA contract. To make space for the third-year wing, the Knicks are waiving Kevin McCullar Jr.

The Knicks weren’t the only team interested either. On Thursday night, rumors indicated that both the Timberwolves and Raptors were also looking at Knecht.

The former 17th overall pick averaged 9.8PPG and 2.8RPG while shooting 46.1% from the field and 37.6% from three during his rookie season. For spurts, it looked like he could develop into a solid rotation piece for a Lakers team that was still trying to contend with LeBron James at the helm and became a fan favorite after a 37-point explosion in the NBA Cup.

Midway through the season, though, Knecht was involved in a trade that would have sent him to the Hornets in exchange for center Mark Williams. After Williams failed his physical and the trade was rescinded, Knecht was forced to return to the Lakers.

Knecht, contrary to belief, finished out the season on a solid note, averaging 8.5PPG while shooting 40.8% from three. Things did take a turn for the worse last season, though. After appearing in 78 games and averaging 19.2MPG in his first season, he averaged just 10.2MPG in just 54 games during the 2025-26 campaign. As many young players do, he struggled with the decreased minutes and inconsistent playing time, leading to a cycle of worse play and even fewer minutes.

The third-year man can still impact the Knicks. He’s just 25 years old and is an above-average shooter with size. In his final year in college, he averaged 21.7PPG on 45.8% shooting from the field and 39.7% shooting from three. It’s not every day you can find that kind of shooting at his height on the waiver wire. But there are plenty of reasons why he saw his minutes dwindle and why he eventually was waived.

Despite being 6’6”, Knecht isn’t much of a defender. He can get lost defensively, and even if he manages to be in the right spots at the right times, he just does not possess the athleticism to be much of a factor on that end. Offensively, he’s shown flashes of being able to utilize his shot to get to other spots on the floor. When a part of the rotation, he was making nice reads off the ball and routinely had nice timely cuts to get easy looks at the rim. But at the end of the day, he’s still best utilized as a spot-up shooter and only a spot-up shooter. He can’t create for himself due to a lack of a reliable handle and certainly doesn’t create for others.

There are also examples of Knecht not knowing the team’s plays and schemes, which would surely frustrate Mike Brown, who is a very detail- and execution-oriented coach.

Knecht is just 25 years old and has room to grow. If the Knicks, their coaches, and their culture get him right, the shooting and size likely give him more upside than McCullar. But don’t expect him to be a significant contributor. New York likely signed him as a project piece and a deep depth piece. It would take a whole lot for Knecht to not only enter the rotation but to stay there. And in such a circumstance, the Knicks would likely have a lot more than Knecht’s play to worry about.

That being said, it’s still an intriguing low-risk move for a player who may just have needed a change of scenery. It is unfortunate, though, to see McCullar gone given the memorable moments he’s had with this club, regardless of how infrequent they may have been.

items.lbText:
Manchester United coach wants ‘humility’ and ‘resilience’

He does not rule out stripping Fernandes of captaincy

Michael Carrick began his Friday media conference with an extraordinary 5min 27sec monologue that cited Manchester United’s values of “humility”, “resilience” and “earning the right to win”, in what could be read as a public address to his players after the season’s dismal start.

The head coach, whose job is under threat , later stated “100%” he could turn United’s form around and sought to underline his selfless attitude by saying he would hold an umbrella for “everyone else to stay dry” while he got wet.

The downpour on Carrick intensified on Wednesday when Bruno Fernandes questioned his tactics after United’s 4-1 Champions League loss at Como and the coach did not rule out dropping the midfielder or stripping him of the captaincy when Bournemouth visit on Sunday. “I’ll always do what’s best for the football club,” he said. “The most important thing for me is the team, first and foremost – the squad, the dynamics in the squad.”

Carrick decided to make his speech, delivered without being asked a question, after events in Como and Lisandro Martínez’s criticism a week earlier of Jason Wilcox for the signings by the director of football.

United have won only two of 11 games and . Carrick said: “We need to respect what it takes to be here, respect what it takes to win, what you have to do to win. I’m not entitled to be here. Entitlement cannot be at this football club. We’re not entitled to win. We’ve won in the past, we’ve got an incredible history, but that doesn’t mean you’re entitled to just win.”

Carrick, a highly decorated United player for 12 years until 2018, cited two of his former teammates. “Ryan Giggs, arguably one of the greatest to play for this club, it was never about Ryan Giggs, it was about Manchester United. Wayne Rooney was top goalscorer of this football club. His biggest thing was playing for the team, sacrificing for the team, and what was good for Manchester United.

“Sir Alex Ferguson, the best manager of all time, the greatest for me … his main priority was Manchester United. Going back to Sir Matt [Busby], Sir Bobby [Charlton], the resilience was beyond belief of what they showed and the way they rebuilt this football club,” referring to the aftermath of the Munich disaster. Carrick insisted he could embody these values and transform United’s campaign. “One hundred per cent, yeah,” he said, before confirming he had spoken to the hierarchy and players about the crisis.

“There’s always conversations going on. It’s pretty obvious how we’re all feeling. The responsibility for me to be in this position is to lead.” Warming to his theme, he said: “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry. That’s the position I’m in and it’s a privileged position.”

Carrick believes all of his squad share his determination – “If you don’t, this is not the place for you,” he said – and insisted there were no factions. “It’s not divided. We just need to get back to doing what we do best and we will.”

items.title: Jolanda Neff Follows Kate Courtney in Latest MTB-to-Road Pivot
items.author: ahood
items.content: Neff joins Courtney in road racing transition as flexible teams and new points rules give top stars more freedom to race across disciplines.
items.lbText:
Jolanda Neff joins Fenix-Premier Tech for 2027. (Photo: Billy Ceusters/Getty Images)

Jolanda Neff joins the growing mini-trend of off-road champions taking their talent to the WorldTour road peloton.

Neff, 33, is heading back to the pavement to join Fenix-Premier Tech in 2027.

“I’m really excited to join Fenix-Premier Tech, a team that unites mountain biking, cyclocross and road racing at a world-class level,” Neff said.

The Tokyo Olympic mountain bike champion is the latest in a growing list of off-road stars exploring what their engines can do inside the road peloton.

Cycling has had a long history of cross-discipline pollination, and the latest iteration has been roadies crossing over to gravel to explore new possibilities in the booming dirt-road race scene.

At the same time, some major off-road stars are coming back to the road.

Neff’s move comes with an important distinction because she isn’t hanging up the mountain bike.

Fenix-Premier Tech offers a structure to allow her to keep her irons hot in road, cyclocross, and MTB.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot led the way for this latest MTB-to-road pivot.

The Frenchwoman returned to road racing with Visma-Lease a Bike in 2025 after stampeding to Olympic MTB gold in Paris.

She promptly won Paris-Roubaix and the Tour de France Femmes . Some comeback. Of course, the former road world champion already knew her way around a peloton.

Kate Courtney is the latest cross-over story.

The American mountain bike world champion won the 2026 U.S. road title and joined FDJ United-Suez in July, turning an experiment on skinny tires into a new career chapter in the WorldTour.

Another top move comes from Axelle Dubau-Prévot — the younger half-sister of Ferrand-Prévot — who is joining SD Worx–Protime on a two-year deal.

She broke out in gravel in 2024-25 and was picked up by EF Education-Oatly, where she raced a mixed program and hit 10th at Liège-Bastogne-Liège in 2026.

The men have plenty of company in the multi-lane discipline craze.

Mathieu van der Poel , Wout van Aert, and Tom Pidcock made crossing disciplines part of their superstar identities.

Of course, nothing is a guarantee even for the world’s most gifted racers. Van der Poel has won world titles in cyclocross, road, and gravel, but he is still chasing mountain biking .

Alan Hatherly joined Jayco-AlUla in 2025 and combined WorldTour racing with his mountain bike ambitions . The idea was to up his overall depth and skillset by pushing into unfamiliar territory.

“I was always interested in road racing and testing my full potential as a cyclist,” Hatherly told Velo in an earlier interview. “I want to keep learning and growing as an athlete. This was the ultimate challenge for me at this point in my career.”

Of course not. Cyclists have been switching lanes ever since people were paid to race bikes.

Taylor Phinney — who raced track and road in his pro career — recently came out of retirement to try to revive USA Cycling’s bid to field a men’s team pursuit squad in track cycling in the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games .

Cadel Evans went from winning MTB World Cups to becoming Australia’s first Tour de France winner.

Traditionally, salaries were much better on the road, but that’s not always the case, especially for the headline off-road stars.

This latest cross-over boom is also fueled by a chance to chase prestigious Olympic medals and world titles in multiple disciplines.

What’s different these days is the flexibility offered from top teams.

In the past, road teams were often reluctant to see their Tour de France stars race over roots and mud for what was perceived as a risk to road ambitions.

That’s changed and several teams are embracing multi-discipline, cross-pollination racing programs.

A recent decision by the UCI to allow points to count across disciplines in team rankings will also give teams an incentive to allow more riders to experiment and compete on any surface.

Neff’s future teammate Puck Pieterse — who won a Tour de France Femmes stage and the elite XCO world title in 2024 — is another rider switching lanes smoothly between road, gravel, cyclocross, and mountain bike.

And all with the full backing of her team.

For Neff — who twice won the Swiss national road title and hit top 10s in world championships and Olympic road racing earlier in her career — the move is her latest challenge.

“I will pour my heart and soul into becoming a better rider in every aspect, as well as sharing all my experience with other riders,” Neff said. “I have always admired how this team puts a strong focus on women and on creating professional structures for them, as well as developing young riders with a long-term vision.”

Gravel remains the favored escape route for roadies right now.

But for ambitious off-road champions, the road is looking just as good coming the other way.

Carrick refuses to rule out dropping Fernandes in emotional address
items.content: <article>Michael Carrick speaks for five uninterrupted minutes at media briefing to outline what Manchester United means to him, then refuses to rule out dropping Bruno Fernandes.</article>
items.lbText:
Under-pressure Manchester United boss Michael Carrick delivered a passionate and emotional address lasting five minutes and 30 seconds as he battles to save his job.

And he refused to rule out dropping skipper Bruno Fernandes for Sunday's Premier League meeting with Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

Instead of taking his seat and answering questions as normal in Friday's scheduled pre-match media conference at Carrington, Carrick said he wanted to start himself.

It was a strategy former boss Sir Alex Ferguson used, although the legendary Scot rarely spoke at such length.

After a run of seven games without a win, culminating in Wednesday's shocking 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como, and attacks on the club's hierarchy by defender Lisandro Martinez and then Fernandes' condemnation of his own tactics in Italy, Carrick wanted to reaffirm his view of what United stood for.

"Recently we haven't had a good time, I think that's pretty obvious," he said.

"Wednesday was a bad night, and it hurt me to see us play like that. It was unacceptable.

"My responsibility is to get a team on the pitch that represents this football club, and the supporters, and they can be proud of in the identity we show. We have gone away from that recently. It's important we all recognise that.

"The foundation and values of this football club have been etched for many years. I totally understand and get every single one of them.

"There's a resilience about this football club that runs very deep. I've seen it with my own eyes, I've felt it, I'm know some of the individuals closely who have been a big part of that history.

"Entitlement cannot be at this football club.

"It was based on being humble, having humility, and hard work. We can never lose that, and I won't let us lose that."

Asked about Fernandes and whether he has considered dropping him, a defiant Carrick added: "The most important thing for me is the team, the squad and dynamics in the squad.

"It's about the football club. I'll always do what is best for the football club."

Conte plays down 'unfounded' Man Utd speculation

Should Man Utd boss Carrick drop captain Fernandes?

Have Man Utd become the unmanageable club?

Club sources said on Thursday Fernandes would not have the captaincy taken away or be fined for his post-match observations following the Como defeat.

In a further interview on Wednesday night with Sky Italia, the Portugal international referred to Manchester United's storied history.

"At this club, there's too much focus on what's been done in the past," said Fernandes. "But we're not those people anymore. The club and the players need to understand that.

"Unfortunately for us - especially when it comes to the players - those who join expect to win trophies, win games, and reach the highest level, that's been very difficult at this club in recent years."

Whether Carrick was aware of Fernandes' comments about United's history before he spoke was uncertain.

When asked again if he would take the captaincy away from the 32-year-old midfielder, Carrick repeated: "I will always do what is best for the football club."

He then refused to say whether he had spoken to Fernandes about his conduct, adding: "I don't think this is the time to go into too much detail."

Despite the challenge to his authority, Carrick said the United dressing room was not divided.

"No, it's not," he added. "We just need to get back to doing what we do best."

Carrick also said the club were 'doing everything' to support Fernandes and his family, whose Cheshire home was burgled on Wednesday.

"Thankfully they weren't directly affected even though it is an awful situation."

Carrick named legendary United figures such as Ryan Giggs, Wayne Rooney and Ferguson as examples of the humility, sacrifice and hard work expected of United players.

That was at odds with his post-match criticism on Wednesday, when he said if you don't run forward or back properly, you will not win games.

Asked how he would persuade his current squad to adhere to the values expected and he demanded, Carrick added: "It's clear as day.

"I'm not telling you anything new. I haven't invented that. That's the make-up of any good football team. You have to earn the right to be better than your opponent. That never changes.

"What we look like as a group is my responsibility. That's the privileged position I am in. I'll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and everyone else to stay dry.

"[Wednesday] hurts an awful lot, but that doesn't stop me. That hurt is used as pure motivation and inspiration to want more, expect more and get us going in a different direction."

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘You’re a freaking perennial All-Star, so just make the bucket’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
The schedule won’t give the Knicks a break as New York visits the Celtics on Friday to fight old pal Mitch Robinson in Beantown.

New York’s off to a losing start to their title-defense season, and going against the also-winless Leprechauns won’t make things easier.

Here’s the latest from your beloved Knickerbockers.

On Andre Drummond’s performance in the Knicks’ season opener against the 76ers:

“I thought he played with a lot of bounce, energy, in the first half on both ends of the floor. We probably ran him too long because it looked like in the second half, not just him but especially our five starters, it looked like he ran out of a little bit of gas. I gotta keep getting to know him to see where the minutes may lie for him to be effective. But I thought he was really, really, really good in the first half.”

On Mitchell Robinson signing with the Celtics and facing him on Friday:

“You’re excited for anybody that’s able to help their situation or family, in life, and Boston gave him a nice deal. And so, you want nothing but the best for him because you know him, and he’s a great, great, great dude. But you wanna beat him at the end of the day.

“So it’s gonna be exciting to see him because of the type of person he is and what we all went through together last year. But at the end of the day, we want to kick his [butt] like he probably wants to kick ours.”

On whether the Knicks might use the Hack-a-Mitch strategy against Mitchell Robinson:

“Me personally, I’ve always leaned more to do that come playoff time or later in the season where you’re really trying to gameplan and get certain games. Right now, I want to see if we can defend these guys with what our foundation is.

“If at some point throughout the course of the game it happens, it happens, but right now I’m just trying to think about communice, be physical without foul, no blow-bys, contest and finish every shot, ball pressure—trying to establish a foundation.”

On Karl-Anthony Towns needing to stop drawing unnecessary fouls:

“Some guys, I say, ‘go try to get fouled,’ Nah nah nah. KAT: You’re a freaking perennial All-Star. So just make the bucket, and if he happens to foul you, then great. When you do those types of [foul-baiting] things, it shortens your opportunities to pick up a foul when you’re boxing out or trying to get a rebound and stuff like that, so that’s the stuff we want to try to eliminate from his game.”

On Towns’ improvement with fouls last season:

“To his credit, he got better as [last] year went along. This is a new year, new team, new challenges.”

On allowing Towns to make mistakes while adjusting to the new season:

“I don’t want him to take 10 steps backwards, but if he takes a couple steps backwards and he’s gotta figure it out, I’m OK with it.”

“There was a three that he shot with Maxey closing out to him. He stuck his leg out. He’s a good enough player to where he doesn’t need to look for and/or try to draw the foul. Just make the basket.”

On staying in the locker room during the Knicks’ championship ceremony:

“I feel like I gotta earn it. I don’t want to experience something that I wasn’t there for.

“I want to be able to experience that [celebration] because I was a part of it. I let those guys have their moment.”

On hearing Knicks fans chant his name at Madison Square Garden:

“It was pretty surreal. Just the energy of the arena, just because of how hard I was working, how hard I was playing, just to hear it, I can’t even really explain it. I got chills. Something you live for as a player, hearing the fans be behind you.

“This arena’s electric. Just doing hard work and aggressive plays gets the crowd going, so it gets me going too.”

On learning Mike Brown’s system and adjusting to his coaching style:

“I think it’s been fun for both of us because, obviously, yes, he’s still trying to get to know me and vice versa, I’m trying to get to know him as a coach. I think we surprise each other on a daily basis on the different things that I’m capable of doing as a player. And obviously, the way his coaching style is too, the freedom I have too, is a little bit different. It’s like a tug-and-pull every time we step on the floor with each other. … It’s cool to have the freedom to play the way I want to play, be able to use my experience and my veteran leadership to play the way I want to play but also play the way he wants me to.”

On feeling welcomed by his new Knicks teammates:

“This is a great team. Great core group. They’ve done a great job of incorporating me into the group and making me feel like I’m one of them.”

On being prepared to step in when Karl-Anthony Towns gets into foul trouble:

“I’m always ready when the moment comes. Obviously, we want KAT to play but whenever my number’s called, I always try to be prepared to go.”

On the Knicks’ 0-1 start and the importance of learning from mistakes:

“It’s Game 1. It means literally nothing. We don’t want to be the best version of ourselves game one – if we are, it’s going to be a long season. A lot of mistakes that we have to learn from.”

On the emotional significance of the Knicks’ championship celebration:

“Something like that, it has a special place in your heart. Now, we’re happy that all of that’s over with and we can fully turn the page and focus on this year.”

On receiving his championship ring in front of Knicks fans at Madison Square Garden:

“It was super dope. A moment you dream of.”

On how the Knicks’ locker room has changed since Mitchell Robinson’s departure:

“It’s definitely different. Obviously that’s someone who’s had a big presence here, big presence in the locker room…No one else listens to country [music] but me, so that’s tough in the weight room. The lack of his presence is obviously felt a little bit. That’s why it’s a new team.”

On the Celtics potentially assigning Robinson to guard him:

“They cross match a lot, so I’m sure he’ll be guarding me, so can’t wait to shoot in that… When I make a couple, I’m gonna let him know.”

On what he expects from the Knicks going against Mitch:

“It’s gonna be the same thing. We’re still gonna be battling for rebounds.”

On facing former Knicks teammate Mitchell Robinson and the Celtics:

“It’s bittersweet. You love Mitch — we’ve done so many historical things together here.

“To not see him in a Knicks jersey anymore…we’re a family unit. To not be able to have him with us on this journey after that amazing journey we went through is bittersweet.

“But it’s going to be amazing to be able to see our brother, hug him, show him some love and compete playing basketball like we love to do. We made each other better. He brought the best out of me, and I feel that I was able to bring the best out of him.

“Mitch was a big part of this team winning a championship and probably has the most important offensive rebound in Knicks history.”

On needing to avoid foul trouble and remain available for his teammates:

“All jokes have some truth to it, right? I never want to put my team in that kind of position — I have to do a better job, not only in the regular season but in the postseason, to make sure I’m available for my team.”

On facing the Knicks for the first time since signing with the Celtics:

“It doesn’t matter that I’m playing my former team. It’s more so just trying to bounce back from what happened two days ago. It’s basketball, it’s a business. Got to play the team just like you play any other team.”

On not watching the Knicks’ championship ring ceremony:

“I didn’t watch it. I mean, I was still stuck in my head (about the opening-day loss)… I’m proud of those guys. Obviously I was a part of it. Didn’t really want to watch it.”

On defending Jalen Brunson and approaching his former teammates like any other opponent:

“Just here to play basketball. Same thing I’ll do with any other team, same thing I’ll do with them. It’s just all about basketball.”

On using the Celtics’ season-opening loss as motivation:

“I use it as fuel, kinda have to. Last game we got demolished. As a big, can’t let that happen. I gotta take that on the chin and learn from it, watch the film, and get better, and just focus on the next one.”

On witnessing the Knicks’ championship ceremony after experiencing a similar moment in Cleveland:

“It was a great night for New York fans. Obviously, it’s something… 50+ years. I was a part of that at one point where we hadn’t won a major championship in Cleveland in over 50 years. The fans will never forget this moment, will never forget that championship run.

“We were happy that we were just able to come and play on such a historical night, a historical building, and play the game we love.”

On defending Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns:

“Obviously, KAT is very dangerous when he has space. Anytime JB is handling the ball with KAT popping, it creates a long closeout for guys trying to get to that shot.”

items.title: Could 71km of time trialing actually help Remco Evenepoel win the Tour de France? A closer look at exactly what the Belgian could gain against Pogačar
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Not since Bradley Wiggins won the 2012 Tour de France have there been as many individual time trial kilometres on the route of cycling's biggest race, with the 71km included on the 2027 route swinging the balance towards the best ITT rider in the peloton and four-time World Champion Remco Evenepoel.

While no route can really be anti-Tadej Pogačar, this is about as good as it can get for the Belgian, with only three summit finishes and almost all of the hardest climbs being backloaded in the second two thirds of the route. Runner-up in 2026 to the Slovenian, Evenepoel will surely be back at the Tour in July, with his eye on at least a repeat GC performance.

Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team boss Ralph Denk didn't go over the top with his assessment of the route and the advantages Evenepoel might seek to gain, but it is clear that a more TT-heavy Grand Tour will always suit his attributes.

"A dream Tour profile for Remco Evenepoel? Hmm, I see that a little differently. More nuanced," he said to at the presentation in Paris, before conceding that, on paper at least, stages 7 and 16 being mostly flat races against the clock should play into their hands.

"In 2012, when Bradley Wiggins won, there were even more than 100. But anyway, it's not bad at all for us, let's say. Remco is currently the very best time trialist in the world, so that is an aspect of this Tour we are certainly going to take into account. That he can gain time on Pogačar, Vingegaard, Seixas and co. in those? In theory, yes."

"The multiple time trial kilometres will provide an extra dimension in any case and make the battle for the yellow jersey more open and exciting," said team Chief of Sports Zak Dempster in agreement.

But how much could the return to more than 70km of individual time trialling – for the first time in 14 years – really benefit Evenepoel in the fight against Pogačar?

Evenepoel only made his Tour debut in 2024, so the three editions he has taken on against the now five-time champion and joint record holder Pogačar have only brought them up against each other in five Grand Tour time trials.

All of those being at the Tour, the score for the moment is 3-2 in the favour of the Belgian, with Pogačar winning the two most climbing-packed stages against the clock in Nice at the end of the 2024 race, and on the pure mountain ITT to Peyragudes in 2025.

Evenepoel has beaten Pogačar to three stage wins at the flatter tests in Gevrey-Chambertin in 2024, Caen in 2025, and Thonon-les-Bains this past season, but the margin has never been major – 12 seconds, 16 seconds, and 28 seconds.

Yes, he has had the advantage – as he should on the completely flat stage 7 to Chambord and stage 16 in Toulouse, even with the viciously steep Côte de Pech David (800m at 12.%) characterising the middle of the route – but it's far from the complete domination that Evenepoel has subjected everyone, including Pogačar, to outside of the Grand Tours.

The image of Evenepoel riding past the usually immortal Slovenian's green jersey during the time trial at the World Championships in Kigali 13 months ago is one which will serve as a symbol of the Belgian's absolute monopoly over the discipline in recent memory, claiming the past four rainbow jerseys.

On that day, the monumental gap between their TT abilities wasn't only apparent in the overtake, but in the time difference at the finish: 2:37.

In fact, across their careers, they have faced off 12 times in individual time trials, Evenepoel winning 10 of them. Only on the two mountain courses at the Tour has he lost to Pogačar to against the clock.

So why does the gap seem to narrow significantly when they are racing in a time trial in the Tour?

The balance swinging massively in Pogačar's favour when an uphill road is included is no surprise – with less aerodynamic advantage for the 'Aero Bullet' Evenepoel at play, due to drag becoming less of a factor at slower speeds, and power-to-weight ratio (W/kg) becoming the more important variable.

But even on the flatter and purer courses, where Evenepoel has long been putting the likes of two-time World Champion Filippo Ganna to shame – most recently by a relatively huge 57 seconds at Worlds in Montreal, Pogačar is much closer during the Tour.

The likely answer comes down to weight, with Evenepoel admitting just this year that he arrived at the Tour almost 4kg down on the weight he had been operating at during the Classics. It's no secret that Evenepoel was in incredible condition for this year's Tour, putting up some of his best climbing performances with victory atop Plateau de Solaison, second on Alpe d'Huez, and keeping up with Pogačar for much longer in the second and third weeks than he has in previous years.

For events like the Worlds TT, where he destroyed Pogačar in Kigali as mentioned, Evenepoel operates at a higher weight, gaining around 1-2kg and losing some of his power-to-weight ratio as he ups the raw power numbers for his favoured discipline.

There's also the factor that no one in the peloton can maintain their level over three weeks like six-time Grand Tour winner Pogačar, whose repeatability and powers of recovery make him the perfect rider to take on punchy finishes, mountain stages and time trials day after day at the Tour – and compete for the win on all of them.

The best benchmark we have for how much time Evenepoel gain across 71 kilometres of time trials is the 28-second deficit he opened up to Pogačar at this year's Tour, over a course of just 26.1km.

Based on their average speeds from that day, 48.85kph for Evenepoel and 47.751kph for Pogačar, a perfect world would see the Belgian cover the 71km 1:05 faster than his rival – not exactly world-beating, but a time trial, with corners, ups and downs, and several accelerations, is far from a perfect world.

Evenepoel's advantage could become greater the longer they have to race, given he has the best aero TT position in the peloton, especially with the 71km being split into a flatter 38km effort, where the Belgian's edge should be magnified as the kilometres tick by. But the steep hill on stage 16 also plays massively into the hands of Pogačar, even at just 800 metres in length, equalising the equation between the pair. ]

The clear conclusion is that Evenepoel cannot rely just on his strongest weapon to truly take down the current benchmark – he will have to beat him, or, at the bare minimum, match him in the high mountains to stay in striking distance for the stages he will almost definitely win.

One other factor that the Belgian newspaper put to Red Bull management is how the arrival of the first mountain stage on stage 9 could help Evenepoel, who really built into his climbing powers this past July after struggling in the opening week.

"That can indeed be an advantage," said Denk. "On the other hand: if you go all out for the general classification, and that is what we always want to do with this team, you also have to be alert in those first ten days and control the situation."

Of his eventual 6:26 deficit to Pogačar in Paris, Evenepoel lost almost three minutes of that on stage 6, the first real big mountain day to Gavarnie-Gèdre. Losing just over three minutes over the remaining 15 stages was a massive step up, and could also play into the hands of the ever-developing Belgian star in his second year with Red Bull, but he'll have to cling onto Pogačar's wheel on stages like the brutal 18th to Col du Portet in a way that only really Jonas Vingegaard has been able to do since 2020 if he wants any hope of yellow.

Conte plays down 'unfounded' Man Utd speculation
items.content: <article>Antonio Conte says he is not in advanced talks with any club, in response to speculation he has held talks with Manchester United. </article>
items.lbText:
Antonio Conte has said he is not in "advanced negotiations" with any club in response to reports he has held talks with Manchester United.

Italian newspaper La Repubblica , external claimed on Thursday that Conte had held talks with United's board about replacing Michael Carrick following the 4-1 defeat against Como on Wednesday.

The report said the former Chelsea manager had demanded full control of United's transfer policy and stated his intention to appoint his own staff at Old Trafford.

But, while BBC Sport understands Conte is keen on the job, the Italian says he is not in "advanced" talks with any club.

"My name has been linked with numerous clubs, but there are currently no negotiations at an advanced stage," Conte wrote on Instagram.

"I have read reports of financial demands and requests for full control that I have supposedly already made to the clubs mentioned, as well as reservations about what has been described as my "strong personality". These reports are unfounded.

"Should a concrete opportunity arise, that will be the time to hold discussions with the club concerned and jointly consider the terms of a potential agreement, with due regard for both parties' needs and the qualities and approach that define my work as a manager."

Carrick's future at Old Trafford is uncertain after a humiliating defeat to Cesc Fabregas' Como in the Champions League earlier this week.

Although Carrick is set to remain in charge for Sunday's Premier League match against Bournemouth, sources have told BBC Sport that United have begun the process of identifying possible replacements.

Former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe, Conte and ex-Germany manager Julian Nagelsmann are all understood to have their eyes on the job.

Conte is a free agent after leaving Napoli at the end of last season.

He won the Serie A title during his first season in Naples, before a Supercoppa Italiana victory in his final campaign.

items.title: 'The race will be wide open' – With no long climbs and no individual time trial, does the 2027 Tour de France Femmes route suit home favourite Pauline Ferrand-Prévot?
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Two summers ago, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot soared to a historic home victory at the Tour de France Femmes, dominating the closing Alpine stages to deliver a first French Tour win in decades and the biggest win of her career.

She beat Demi Vollering by almost four minutes in Châtel, but this year the tables turned as Ferrand-Prévot endured a disastrous title defence, losing minutes in the Dijon time trial before falling out of contention in the Ardèche hills and conceding defeat on Mont Ventoux.

Clearly, a rider of Ferrand-Prévot's calibre is better than her early-August performance, and the Visma-Lease a Bike star will aim to bounce back next year. But is the 2027 Tour de France Femmes route one where she can thrive and take back the yellow jersey from Vollering?

Well, race director Marion Rousse delivered both good and bad news for the 34-year-old and her team in the Palais des Congrès in Paris on Thursday afternoon.

For a start, there's no individual time trial on next year's route. That will be music to Ferrand-Prévot's ears after she lost two minutes to Vollering and Marlen Reusser over just 21km on the road to Dijon in August.

Ferrand-Prévot was always expected to shed time against the clock, even as her team protested how much she had trained on the TT bike, so for a start, she's already looking at several minutes saved. Coming in place of an individual time trial, however, is a team test in the form of a flat 18km tour of central London.

Team time trials are rare in women's cycling, with next year's stage a first in Tour de France Femmes history. The other Grand Tours have featured a TTT in recent history, though, with the Giro featuring one in 2021 and the Vuelta doing so between 2022 and 2025.

Do Visma have the personnel to succeed in such a test? Time will tell, and it's impossible to make any predictions this far out, but in former time trial specialist Jos van Emden, they have a directeur sportif well-placed to guide them in London.

"The team time trial is a notable feature. It’s an event we haven't seen before in the Tour de France Femmes," Van Emden said after the route unveiling.

"I'm a fan of team time trials. We haven't raced many of them as a team, so it's difficult to make any immediate predictions about our collective strength or the course in London. You have to master every discipline if you want to win the Tour. This will be another new challenge.

"That decision shows that women's cycling is continuing to evolve and grow in importance. A team time trial is part of what makes the Tour the Tour, as it’s the biggest stage in cycling."

Is there enough climbing for PFP?

The goal will likely be to limit losses and keep Ferrand-Prévot close to her main yellow jersey rivals as the race hits France, with the opening two stages in the north of England unlikely to have produced much in the way of GC gaps.

On the mainland, it will all be about surviving the pitfalls of the sprint stages and then overcoming the tricky, punchy hills on the road to Magnanville on stage 5.

The big time differences, however, should be made in the final three days as the race reaches the Massif Central, though there are no long Alpine climbs on the menu here like the Madeleine, where Ferrand-Prévot built her 2025 Tour victory with that dominant solo ride.

Will that be a problem for the lightweight climber?

"The first thing that stands out to me is how different this Tour is from the editions in recent years. The high mountains are missing. That was certainly different in previous editions," Van Emden said.

Stage 7 features a closing climb to La Loge des Gardes (6.7km at 7.1%), while the mid-mountain stage 8 to Clermont-Ferrand features the Côte de Charade (6km at 5.9%) before a descent to the finish. The showpiece final stage concludes atop the Puy de Dôme, which measures 11.3km at an average gradient of 7.8%.

Van Emden said that the Tour is no easier than the recent editions, even if the Puy de Dôme stage doesn't quite measure up to the recent queen stages of the Glandon-Alpe d'Huez in 2024, the Madeleine last year, or the Ventoux in August.

"The longest climb in this Tour is 11km. That was different in recent years. But that doesn’t mean this will be an easier Tour," he said.

"Quite the opposite: the race will be wide open, and the general classification contenders will be fighting for every second in every stage.

"That’s a very special way to finish. In cycling, this climb may not be as well known as Mont Ventoux or the Col de la Madeleine, which featured in recent editions, but that’s also because it’s a protected natural area. I’m really looking forward to finishing atop the volcano."

As is the case for the men's race, there's clearly one standout favourite for next year's Tour de France Femmes – the defending champion. This Tour route certainly isn't built with Ferrand-Prévot in mind, but success isn't out of reach, and if she's back on form, next August could well host the Ferrand-Prévot vs Vollering battle we've been waiting for.

Between now and then, there's plenty of time for training, planning, and recon rides. The planning will get underway soon, said Van Emden.

"We’ll draw up our plans this winter. With Pauline, we have the 2025 Tour winner on our team, although she would normally be better suited to the longer climbs.

"But we have several cards to play. I think this route suits us very well. It’s going to be an explosive Tour."
