items.lbText:
The reigning champions must deal with the absence of Khvicha Kvaratskhelia for some time, while fans at Anfield were thrilled by Rio Ngumoha

Paris Saint-Germain beat Barcelona 4-2 on Tuesday , but the reigning champions lost the best player in last season’s tournament, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. This autumn has seen much lobbying for the Ballon d’Or, with the Georgian a popular choice, despite his absence from the World Cup. He is expected to be out for six months, although Rodri’s comeback from serious injury – he was rested by Barcelona on Tuesday until coming off the bench in the 60th minute – shows it can take far longer than that for players to rediscover their highest level.

“Why me?” Kvaratskhelia asked his Instagram followers. The PSG policy of resting players in Ligue 1 to save them for the Champions League failed to protect him. By resting Rodri, Barcelona followed a wider practice among major clubs in European competition of saving stars’ legs for big domestic occasions. Barcelona face Real Madrid this weekend though Lamine Yamal is not being spared; his brilliant goal in Paris made it 10 goals, matched by 10 assists, from 10 matches.

Another heavyweight battle saw Arsenal lose Bukayo Saka to a first-half quad injury in an entertaining 2-2 draw at Bayern Munich . Declan Rice powered in a late equalizer after Harry Kane had put on a show that included a goal and an assist. Does the Ballon d’Or beckon for Kane? The prediction markets suggest so.

Matching Barcelona’s perfect record this season at home and abroad are Manchester City, who continue to thrive amid infamy. A resurgent Phil Foden scored a hat-trick and new signing Allan impressed. The official crowd for their 5-1 defeat of AEK Athens was 40,402, but it looked smaller, and mockery duly descended on the club. There is mitigation for those who stayed away, including high ticket prices for Champions League matches in tough economic times, and a run of five home matches in 17 days. Still, City remain in the crosshairs, and the empty seats raise eyebrows for a club reporting record revenues. Equally, it is fair to point out that Anfield was not full, either, for Liverpool’s 4-3 defeat of Villarreal.

A clean sweep of wins for Serie A, with three of their clubs scoring four goals. Inter let the side down with their 1-0 defeat of Shakhtar Donetsk. Roma defeated Slovan Bratislava 4-0, and Como beat Manchester United 4-1 , but the game of the week came in Naples. Scott McTominay scored twice, his first goals since a procedure on a benign heart arrhythmia as Napoli beat Bodø/Glimt 4-3 for their first win of the group stage. “I still need to find my best form, but I am not far away,” said McTominay.

Liverpool were a mess in the first 30 minutes against Villarreal and it was Rio Ngumoha who led the recovery. The 18-year-old played off the right, supplying two assists with his left foot: the long-term replacement for Mohamed Salah may already be at Anfield. Liverpool have nursed Ngumoha along, though this was his fifth start of the season. “Everyone is chipping in but for him to work with Mo [Salah] last year was obviously massive,” Virgil van Dijk said of the teenager.

With traditional Serie A giants Juventus and Milan in the Europa League, Como are enjoying their first season in the Champions League. If Manchester United were dreadful on Wednesday, Como’s rise hit its highest point yet. The club’s success carries echoes of Brighton and Bournemouth’s ascents, although Como’s is even more remarkable. They were a Serie D club in 2008, and the city is now known for something beyond its glorious scenery. Champions League winner Thierry Henry is among the investors in the club as is Como’s coach, Cesc Fàbregas, although the prime financiers are the Indonesian billionaire Hartono brothers.

Jamestown Analytics, the Brighton owner Tony Bloom’s company, has been consulting Como . Arsène Wenger, Pep Guardiola, José Mourinho and Antonio Conte are the elite coaches Fàbregas played under, and he has forged a high-pressing style against Italian orthodoxy. As United labored, they were swarmed by Como’s worker bees. Real Madrid have a buy-back option for Nico Paz, bought by Como in 2024, and the scorer of two fine goals against United. Argentina’s latest Messi replacement is rather beefier than his country’s idol.

As Como deepened Michael Carrick’s plight, thoughts moved to potential replacements. Fàbregas has been mentioned, though United fans will recall the summer of 2013’s unsuccessful chase for him. Had a deal been done, his midfield partner would have been … Carrick.

Another week, another Manchester United PR crisis. This one involved Carrick hitting back at his players, a rarity in his managerial career. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” Bruno Fernandes said.

Carrick’s riposte: “If you don’t run and you don’t run forward and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win.”

On CBS, Jamie Carragher weighed, saying of Fernandes: “They all think he’s working hard. He’s not. He’s killing the rest of the team doing it.”

The Amazon All or Nothing documentary series currently in production for United’s season will be appointment viewing.

After two consecutive weeks of action, we have a fortnight off. Will Carrick still be at United by the time they host Roma on 3 November? Aston Villa, who have three wins from three and are second place in the table, have a glamour trip to Barcelona . Real Madrid, another side on three wins, travel to AEK.

After defeat to Inter, Shakhtar’s adopted home, Stamford Bridge , hosts Sporting Lisbon, who this week were on the wrong end of Lask’s first ever group-stage win.

items.title: Gear up for wet weather winter riding – Our best budget waterproof jacket has 15% off, making it even better value for money

items.title: The Best Gifts for Biking Families
items.author: Emily LaPointe
items.content: Give 'em more two-wheel fun with these eight products
items.lbText:
If there’s one thing most adventure-loving families can agree on, it’s this: bikes do it all, from thrill rides to zipping over to a friend’s house to the school or work commute. Luckily, there’s never been a better time to raise a biker, thanks to the wide range of children’s cycling gear out there. These eight products from REI make awesome holiday gifts for aspiring shredders, from bikes to packs to safety equipment. The only catch? Better be prepared to get on your own bike and chase these well-outfitted kids around.

For young kids learning to ride, the key is having the right bike at the right time, so they can build skills and confidence. Built for young riders ages 3 to 5, the REV 14 from REI Co-op is the perfect intermediate step between a balance bike and a real-deal frame. The design allows for balance bike-style riding, but the REV pedals are fully functional (it’s also training-wheel compatible). Front and rear handbrakes teach speed control, an easily adjustable seat accommodates fast-growing kids, and the sturdy aluminum frame is hand-me-down durable.

The best kids’ gear fits and performs just as well as the adult equivalent, and that’s exactly what the Moki 3 does. It’s sized for children (ages 4 to 12), but its design, materials, comfort, and functionality are adult level. The Moki 3 includes breathable mesh shoulder straps and a light foam backpanel, as well as a 1.5-liter hydration reservoir. The Moki’s spacious main compartment and zippered front pocket can hold everything your little one needs, from layers to snacks to their favorite toy.

Here’s a great parent problem to have: You need to train to keep up with your burgeoning speed demon. If that’s a reality for someone on your list, this bike trainer is the answer. The KICKR Core 2 is compatible with most 8- to 13-speed bikes, and its highly customizable design means users can dial in the right amount of resistance and build a super-effective workout. With an intuitive interface and integrated WiFi, the KICKR simplifies getting stronger when outdoor riding isn’t on the day’s agenda.

Once the training wheels come off, the most exciting gift a kid can receive is a “big kid” bike of their very own. The REV 20 from REI Co-op is the perfect upgrade, thanks to components that are designed specifically for riders ages 6 to 9, as well as smart features. Those include a freewheel wheel that lets kids get accustomed to backpedaling and front and rear handbrakes. The REV 20 also includes a sticker pack, reinforcing rule number one: Bikes are fun!

Actually, there’s another rule number one in biking: safety. Giro packs a ton of tech into this child-size helmet, kitting it out with a Mips liner (which reduces rotational forces), EPS foam covered by a hard polycarbonate shell, and 13 vents that provide airflow when your little one is putting the pedal to the metal. The Roc Loc® Jr. adjustment system makes finding the right fit simple. Protection is top notch, but what kids will love is the Scamp’s snazzy colors, which will have adults coveting this lid themselves.

For the youngest riders, a balance bike is the way to get started, and this one will get any tyke zooming around in no time. A self-stabilizing wobble effect keeps everything upright, and the toddler-size design fits little arms and legs (the recommended age is 9 to 36 months). With cute colors and an included plushy toy friend who can tag along on adventures, the WOW points the way toward a bright biking future.

It’s hard to disguise a bike with wrapping paper, but that won’t matter when your kid unboxes this well-built bike for riders ages 4 to 6. Everything from its handlebar grips to its mini V-brakes to its aluminum frame is constructed to make for a simple, confident learning experience. The GO 3’s 16-inch aluminum wheels are also outfitted with chunky tires, so some light off-roading might be on the menu once your aspiring ripper gains skills and confidence.

Take Smith’s classic mountain bike helmet design, make it child-friendly while retaining all its safety and design features, and you have the Sidekick Jr. A Mips system reduces rotational forces caused by angled impacts and 12 vents provide plenty of airflow for riding hard on hot days. The dial system is made for kid-size fingers so they can easily adjust fit for comfort. With an integrated visor and liner and two sizes, this is a full-featured helmet for kids who love to ride.

REI is a specialty outdoor retailer, headquartered near Seattle. The nation’s largest consumer co-op, REI is a growing community of 26 million members who expect and love the best quality gear and outstanding customer service. REI is a purpose-driven and values-led company dedicated to enabling life outside for all.

items.title: The bipolarity of Andre Drummond was on full display on Opening Night
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
One game down, 81 to go. How’s everyone feeling?

You don’t feel well? Chin up; here’s something to cheer you up.

There we are. That’s why we don’t get bent out of shape over individual regular-season games anymore.

There truly wasn’t much to really evaluate from the first game of the season, which acted more as a showcase for the league of Philadelphia’s new starting five and the pizzazz around the Knicks’ banner raising than anything meaningful.

I mean, it was the worst offensive execution of any game this team has played in the 2020s, so unless these guys had the basketball ability sucked out of them like the Monstars at the parade, whatever.

Of all the things that happened on the floor on Opening Night, none intrigued me more than the newest Knick, Andre Drummond. We saw a lot from him due to Karl-Anthony Towns’ early foul trouble.

Early in the game, he looked like the biggest steal of the offseason, posting a double-double with ease and carrying the offense at times.

Late in the game, he was the worst player on the court, throwing away possessions with his poor touch around the rim.

Ladies and gentlemen, from the creators of the “Jameis Winston Experience”, I present to you:

The Andre Drummond Experience.

He wows with some of the best traits you can ask for out of a center. He is one of the best rebounders in NBA history on a rate basis; he sets brick-wall screens, he fills up space. While he’s not a good defender, he’s a lane-clogger on defense.

Then, there’s the flip side. His touch around the rim is diabolically bad. His stocky build makes him an extremely limited defender and a non-existent lob threat. While he’s started working on corner threes, he is still almost exclusively an under-the-rim offensive player.

It’s those two things that separate him from a Mitchell Robinson. While he’s historically more durable than Robinson, he doesn’t give the Knicks the game-breaking defensive ability without putting pressure on the rim. That fast break where Mikal Bridges tried to hit him on a lob, not realizing the 33-year-old can’t really get up there anymore, said everything.

Drummond is good in small doses. It’s why he’s forced to sign these minimum contracts to sit behind All-NBA talents like Joel Embiid and Towns. When you over-expose him, the bad starts to show up a lot more than the good.

We got the full Drummond experience on Tuesday. He had 10 points, 12 rebounds, 3 assists, and 3 stocks in 16 first-half minutes, going 4-for-8 from the field with six offensive rebounds. He was a maniac on the boards, punishing a Sixers team with not much size and not many willing rebounders.

Considering how little they had at their disposal, the Knicks couldn’t have done much better than Drummond in free agency. A lot of their offense over the last few years has been predicated on winning the possession battle. When they miss a three, someone is there to give them a reload. When they miss at the rim, there’s a putback waiting to happen.

When Drummond is on the floor, it’s going to be like Mitch never left offensively… most of the time.

The one glaring problem with having Drummond as your backup center behind a guy like Towns who gets in early foul trouble way too often is that his overexposure really starts to hurt you.

He played a grand total of six minutes in the second half and was a minus-13. He went 1-for-5 from the field, including an airball in the final seconds of the third quarter.

His minutes at the end of the third were especially damaging. The Knicks were leading by five when he entered the game with 3:39 left and trailed by seven when the final horn sounded.

What went wrong? His eyes got too wide offensively.

He and Bridges had a two-man game around the two-minute mark. It looked to be working in the sense that it allowed Mikal to hit him on a bounce pass for what should be an easy floater or rim run, but the Sixers rotated two guys underneath the basket. At this point, Drummond could look up and swing to a wide open OG Anunoby or Deuce McBride.

Instead, he takes a nine-footer that isn’t even close.

Drummond is a very willing passer, especially on offensive rebounds, but plays like these still happen for all seldom-used bigs.

The Knicks were starting to be grilled from deep by a collection of Sixers. Trailing by four in the final minute, Drummond gets the ball in the corner. For a brief second, I thought he would shoot it. It’s not a great shot with 14 on the shot clock, but he’s open and was a passable three-point shooter last season.

Instead, he passed back and the Knicks once again stagnated offensively. He was given a pass in the post with seven on the shot clock, but the defense collapsed and it led to him taking… this shot.

I’m not expecting him to have eyes in the back of his head, but unless it’s a grenade, he should never be attempting whatever that is. All it does is give more energy to your opponent.

After Tyrese Maxey airballed, the Knicks got the ball with 1.5 on the game clock. For some reason, McBride, the former high school quarterback, decided to throw a 50-foot pass to his backup center down the court and airmailed it. This isn’t Drummond’s fault (why was he even out there?), but it involves him.

Jaylen Brown nailed a buzzer-beating three there to cap an 11-0 run to end the third. That sprint by the Sixers wound up costing the Knicks the game.

This stretch doesn’t even include his three baffling missed dunks. He was routinely getting stuffed by Joel Embiid on the interior and couldn’t finish all game, going 5-for-13 on the night.

That is the big crux for Drummond: he is an abysmal finisher for a seven-footer, and he’s progressively getting worse.

Andre Drummond FG% in the restricted area by year, and where he ranked among centers (min. 100 FGA):2025-26: 54.1% (61st/61)2024-25: 59.2% (59th/60)2022-23: 65.5% (56th/64)

Compare that to who he’s replacing in Robinson: the man who has the second-highest field goal percentage in NBA history on a diet of 100% layups and dunks. In 2025-26, Robinson was 25th out of the 61 centers, which doesn’t sound impressive, but his 71.9% is leaps and bounds ahead of Drummond’s dead-last figure.

All told, Knicks fans are going to have a love-hate relationship with Drummond all season long, a man who says the right things and is good natured, but is also the Jameis Winston of the NBA.

An incredibly entertaining, but incredibly inconsistent, ballplayer.

items.title: Coros Dura 2 Solar Review: The Infinite-Battery Garmin Alternative (And the Detail Everyone Will Miss)
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: The 120-hour battery life and ultra-thin design steal the spotlight. But the real reason to consider this head unit has nothing to do with how long it lasts.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Unique look Lighter than other comparable computers Excellent backend training infrastructure Fast rerouting and general operation Ability to schedule ride tracking Exceptionally long battery life Fantastic music player integration Uses a standard Garmin style mount 2-1 Solar gain (two hours of battery life for every hour of ride time) The best Strava live segments implementation

Lacks third party integrations Ecosystem is a walled garden Screen brightness and resolution lacking

Most people knew the original Coros Dura because it was cheap and had an incredible battery life. Today, the Coros Dura 2 launches and it’s not cheap anymore, but it brings a lot to the table. Among those things is a form factor that is unlike anything else on the market.

Of course, part of me wants to say that form factor doesn’t matter, but come on, let’s be real here—this is pretty cool. The new Coros Dura 2 Solar has a carbon fiber backplate and an anodized aluminum bezel making up what sort of looks like two pieces that stack together. The leading edge is only 5.7mm thick and looks more like a concept bike computer than real life.

It is real, though, and it works because it stacks on top of a rear section that houses a pair of buttons, the USB-C charging port, a speaker, and the solar panel. That solar panel has its own set of pressure-sensitive buttons, meaning they respond to actual physical force rather than just the light electrical touch of your finger like a smartphone screen. You’ll also find the Garmin-compatible quarter-turn mount housed in the rear section, and when you put it all together, it’s genuinely unique and very cool to look at.

The new computer isn’t just a pretty face, though. Coros has been mounting a genuine challenge to Garmin for the last few years, and this latest computer is yet another part of that narrative while also bringing unique features to market. To test it all out, I took off my Garmin watch, strapped on a Coros Pace 4 Pro, put the Garmin Edge 1050 in a drawer, and mounted the Coros Dura 2 Solar on my bars. Here’s what I found out.

There are several pillars I want to discuss regarding the Coros Dura 2 Solar, but the battery life is so far beyond what anyone else is offering that it has to be addressed first. It almost minimizes how much Coros outpaces the competition to merely list battery life as “a feature I like” in our standard Velo review format.

Currently, the longest battery life for a direct competitor is the Garmin Edge 1060, which carries a 20-hour rating for regular use and 60 hours in battery-saver mode. You could also point to the Garmin 1040 Solar and its 180-hour rating, but that comes with heavy caveats. First, it is two generations old, despite still being available. Second, that 180-hour figure requires solar charging and zero paired sensors; use it like a normal computer, and it drops to 45 hours. Both are decent numbers given the next closest option is the Wahoo Elemnt Ace with a claim of up to 30 hours.

Then there’s Coros. The Coros Dura 2 Solar isn’t just knocking it out of the park; this computer is playing a completely different sport. The baseline rating is 120 hours if you drop the GPS to single-band, or 70 hours in the more accurate dual-frequency mode. More importantly, those numbers are calculated without solar charging.

Coros claims—and I have no reason to doubt it—that the solar panel will generate two hours of ride time for every hour spent in direct sun. That means if you operate this like a normal bike computer in 2026, fully connected to sensors and actively navigating, you may never actually have to plug it in. After six hours of riding, all with the backlight turned to 100%, and multiple days sitting indoors—Coros designed the unit to stay in standby rather than powering down completely—my review unit was sitting at 93%. I stopped checking the battery percentage after that.

Focusing exclusively on the battery life does sell the Dura 2 slightly short, however. When the original Dura launched, it felt half-finished and was not a great product. Velo actually published a second first-impressions article when later firmware updates finally made it a reasonable option, but it still lagged behind the competition.

With the launch of the Dura 2, Coros is shedding that legacy. Every manufacturer has advantages and disadvantages, but if you want a reliable head unit in 2026, the Coros Dura 2 is firmly in the “yes, this is a good computer” category. A significant part of that success comes down to the ecosystem.

Because I like to self-coach, performance tracking and recovery metrics are important to me. Garmin has been the king of that space for years with Garmin Connect. However, Garmin operates a walled garden, and the hardware buy-in is expensive. Coros clearly recognized this market opportunity. The Coros Training Hub is every bit as good, and while it is also a walled garden—albeit one that allows Wahoo head units inside—the hardware is significantly cheaper. I am a big fan of the simple recovery status, as well as the implementation of metrics that mirror Joe Friel’s gold-standard CTL, ATL, and TSB models in TrainingPeaks.

A bike computer is just one piece of an overall training ecosystem but this is a solid one. I prefer a single upfront hardware purchase rather than paying recurring subscription fees for training software over time. Coros nails that, and the Dura 2 is a key piece of the puzzle.…

items.title: Coros launches futuristic Dura 2 Solar computer with monster battery life and built-in voice control
items.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
items.content:
Coros has launched the new Dura 2 Solar bike computer today, in what is a major update to the brand's original Dura model, which launched in 2024.

The original Dura made waves when it launched thanks to its solar charging technology, which provided at least a 120-hour battery life, making the unit popular with long-distance riders or those who wanted to cut down on regular charging.

The Dura 2 Solar maintains the same claimed 120-hour battery life from a single charge, not including solar power and 2:1 solar regeneration (meaning you gain two hours of battery for every hour of sun exposure) that the original unit had, and there's been a major overhaul everywhere else.

The unit has been redesigned into a slicker, lighter package; the old digital dial is gone, and the hardware has been given a major upgrade.

In short, the Dura 2 Solar seems to be a far more premium overall package that looks more capable of taking the fight to the big hitters when it comes to the best bike computers.

Something else that has changed is the price: the Dura 2 has a retail price of $499 / £429 / €499, a healthy amount more than the previous unit's RRP of $249 and comes without a mount.

The unit uses a horizontal quarter-turn standard (Garmin mount), and the brand argues most riders already have a mount, or need a specific one anyway for their bike's handlebars.

A computer and mount option is available for $549 / £479 / €549, and standard and out-front mounts are available for $79 / £69 / €79.

The unit will be available for purchase from the 27th of October. We understand the original Coros Dura unit will be phased out from this point.

We have everything we know so far here on the computer, as well as our first impressions after logging some rides with the new unit.

Carbon fibre, aluminium and solar power

The Dura 2 Solar looks radically different to the outgoing unit; it's now lighter than before at a claimed 99 grams and uses a T700 carbon fibre backplate and aluminium alloy in its construction.

The front half of the unit is incredibly thin at just 5.7mm, whilst the solar charging panels have been moved to the bottom of the computer. There are two buttons on either side of the computer body, as well as a USB-C charging port on the right-hand side. There are also two new haptic buttons which can be found on the solar panel as well.

The screen is now bigger; the Dura 2 has a 3.5" Sharp MIP (memory-in-pixel) colour touchscreen, an increase over the old unit's 2.7" screen. Coros has provided some details. The screen has a 17:9 aspect ratio and 201 pixels per square inch.

Like the Garmin Edge 1060 computer that launched this week, the Dura 2 also has a voice control feature. Pressing both buttons on the side of the unit activates the voice control feature, which can be toggled on and off.

The unit, as you might expect, is WiFi, ANT+, and Bluetooth-friendly and works with GPS, GLONASS, GALILEO, BDS and QZSS satellite systems. The brand promises improved routing, pinch-to-zoom screen mapping, climb alerts, and offline re-routing.

Routes can be built in the Coros companion app, which also supports a workout planner and training metric analytics features.

There's also a built-in bike bell, media and camera control functionality, and the ability to upload to ChatGPT and Claude for training analysis.

Shimano and SRAM drivetrain support is built in, and Coros says Campagnolo compatibility will come at the end of the year. Third-party app connections can also be made to the likes of Zwift, Wahoo, Strava, Ride with GPS, Komoot, TrainingPeaks and TrainerRoad.

I've been riding with the Dura 2 for a little while and have logged five hours on the unit so far. Aesthetically, it looks pretty cool, sleek and thoroughly modern, the very thin-to-normal body design perhaps looks slightly disjointed, but that's being really picky.

On the lack of a mount coming with the unit, I see no issue. Most riders will have a Garmin-type mount already, and may likely have their own bike specific out-front mounts sorted anyway. It's one less mount in the spares box in my eyes.

After my initial shakedown ride, I fully charged the Dura 2 and, to test the battery, will use it without recharging until I need to.

After five hours of riding and five days of use, I am at 92.9% battery, with a 0.9% solar charge. You can put the unit into sleep mode in about three seconds, or fully turn it off; I've left it asleep for days at a time.

I've been riding with the screen brightness on full, and with PM and HRM sensors paired, for context. It seems safe to say the battery life is considerably bigger than anything else on the market, like the previous unit.

Initially, at unboxing, I was left disappointed by the unit's screen brightness and overall resolution, noting it to be not as vivid or bright as the Karoo or premium Garmin models. In use, this has been less of an issue than I thought it would be, and outdoors on max screen brightness, the screen is perfectly acceptable to me.

The unit is also fast, one of my colleague Josh's key complaints regarding the original Dura was that it was a touch laggy. The touchscreen is very fast and simple to use, as is the overall user interface and processing speed; no issues from me there.

The map layout looks very good, clearer than Garmin units for me, and up there with the best units around. I'm yet to fully test the navigation features, though.

My only other minor issues at this point are that I can't quite figure out how to get my main road activity profile exactly as I want it, and the lap notification screen takes too long to get rid of, but those things will get answered in time.

I'm already grinning at not having to plug the thing in or check the battery, and the unit is proving to be very capable; it also looks darn pretty cool mounted on your bars. Watch this space for a full review.

items.title: Breaking down Man Utd's tactics after Fernandes' criticism
items.content: <article>Was Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes correct in his analysis of his side's tactics in their 4-1 thrashing by Italian side Como?</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes appeared to question their tactical approach after Wednesday's 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como.

"We started off on the wrong foot," the Portuguese said. "They scored very early, [we had] not much pressure on the ball.

"It's a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave some space behind, to try and get the ball in the first moment [by] waiting for them, [giving] them the ball.

"Sometimes when you give too much of the ball to these teams, they get confidence. They have so many bodies behind the ball, they make you run a lot, people get frustrated."

His quotes are tactically dense so warrant breaking down, but what did Fernandes mean, and does he have a point?

Since Michael Carrick became United manager in January, they have largely defended in a zonal 4-2-4 or 4-4-2 shape that springs into a press in moments.

When Fernandes said United "leave some space behind, to try and get the ball in the first moment" he was referring to them not immediately pressing across the pitch in a man-to-man fashion.

Holding their 4-2-4 shape a little bit deeper, United allow opposition defenders time and space on the ball, looking to set traps before pouncing.

The overarching idea is with four players narrow and high, United's attackers are well positioned to score from turnovers should they win the ball back.

At times during Carrick's stint as caretaker head coach last season, it worked well - as we saw when Bryan Mbeumo scored in United's 3-2 win at Arsenal in January two weeks after Carrick took over

But the same approach has been less effective this season.

On the same night defender Lisandro Martinez questioned United's recruitment - after their 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid - he also spoke about the ever-changing tactical landscape.

"You can't stay with what you did last season." he said. "Teams know you, how you play, know every detail, and if you don't change, next season is a big problem."

Last season, the introduction of the 4-2-4 shape as a defensive tactic caught a number of teams off guard, making it more effective.

Pep Guardiola and Pep Lijnders used the same shape at Manchester City - a tweak that underpinned their Carabao Cup final win over an ill-prepared Arsenal .

Having replaced Guardiola, Enzo Maresca redeployed it for the Community Shield in August, but this time Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta had the solutions and the Gunners won.

Within a few games, Maresca had abandoned the 4-24 and moved to a more man-to-man style of defending.

Perhaps that is the sort of change Fernandes is hoping for - recognising the reduced effectiveness of United's defensive approach, with signs of weakness visible as early as pre-season.

AC Milan - now managed by former United boss Ruben Amorim - repeatedly found joy playing around the 4-2-4, with a back five that outnumbered the Red Devils' front four.

United's two central attackers would look to block passes into Milan's midfield two before pressing the central defenders.

The wide position of one of the central defenders would force a United winger to step out, and Milan's wing-back - dropping deep and wide - gave them an easy way out.

United's full-back would then have to cover a large distance to close down the wing-back but by the time pressure was applied, the ball was gone.

The same problems were seen in United's defeat by Atletico Madrid.

Atletico took the risk of employing the same tactic with a back four rather than a back five, which left them an extra attacker high up the pitch.

As United's front two looked to stop passes into the central midfielders, the wide position of the centre-backs drew out United's wingers.

That, in turn, meant left-back Alejandro Grimaldo found himself in space out wide.

This required Diogo Dalot, or if he was pinned back by winger Alex Baena, Youri Tielemans to cover large distances in an attempt to apply some pressure to Grimaldo.

So while Fernandes may have been referring to himself when he said "they make you run a lot, people get frustrated", it could easily have applied to these team-mates.

When Fernandes' quotes were put to Carrick after the game, he pushed back.

"We actually half-pressed, man-to-man in the second half and then ended up conceding a goal from that," he said.

"It's a little bit on whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, but if you don't run and you don't run forward and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."

While the less aggressive 4-2-4 has its weaknesses, it often leaves an extra player in the backline, giving United a numerical advantage in defence.

It also aims to funnel attacks down the flanks, where they are - in theory - less dangerous than chances conceded through the middle.

United's backline have also - under both Carrick and Amorim - struggled to track and duel with their opponents in one-against-one situations when they have committed to a full press.

When using a man-to-man press, losing an individual battle, or lacking the intensity to arrive at your opposing player quickly, makes the system fall apart as we saw for Como's second goal.

In the Premier League, United have also had spells during which they have attempted to press in a more man-to-man fashion, but these have also been imperfectly executed.

In fact, against Spurs , it was Fernandes who misread moments and positioned himself incorrectly.

Despite Amorim's flaws, one of his strengths was in improving United's physical base and intensity. There is a question as to whether Carrick's United, with one game a week last season, were beneficiaries of that.

This season they look unable to sustain the intensity to execute a man-to-man press with the effectiveness of, say, Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton - a physically fit squad aligned on how and when to press.

For United, more concerningly, there appears to be a disconnect - at least in how Fernandes sees the game and the messaging from the coaching staff.…

items.title: Chris Froome predicts a 'closer' Tour de France in 2027
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Four-time Tour de France winner Chris Froome believes we may see a closer contest for the yellow jersey, as he offered his initial take on the 2027 route that was unveiled in Paris on Thursday.

The route features the heaviest dose of time trialling since 2012, when Froome was the runner-up behind his teammate and compatriot Bradley Wiggins, a podium that would preface four Tour titles in the space of five years.

The 71 kilometres of time trialling are not exactly balanced out by a huge dose of mountains, with two stages in the Alps and two in the Pyrenees, and plenty of punchier terrain in between.

For Froome, Tadej Pogačar remains the favourite to win a record sixth title, but might not run away with it in the same way he has in the past three years.

"It is, as usual, a brutal Tour de France. There is really a bit of everything," said Froome, who was in attendance in the Palais des Congrès in Paris and gave his take to the gathered media, including , behind the stage.

"There are more time trial kilometres, that’s also interesting. We have seen the difference Tadej has made in the mountains so maybe with the time trials we’re going to see a bit of a closer race between the favourites. That will change the approach to the race."

Still, it might not change the favourite, with Pogačar already surpassing Froome's four titles with his record-equalling fifth this summer.

"It's just incredible what Tadej has been doing these past few years," Froome said. "I imagine that next year he’ll be lining up as the main favourite for the Tour de France and no doubt going in to challenge for number six."

Froome was also asked about the Grand Départ, which takes place in his home nation of Great Britain, starting in Edinburgh, Scotland and making its way through England and into the Welsh capital of Cardiff before the hop over to France.

"If it’s anything like it was in 2014, the start over in Scotland is going to be amazing," said Froome, who rode as the defending champion the last time the Tour started in Britain, in Yorkshire, 12 years ago.

"The first three stages on UK soil is going to be be something really special. If it’s anything like 2014 it will just be millions and millions of people who come out.

"I never saw a Grand Départ of a Tour de France that was bigger than 2014 so I imagine next year is going to be similar. A lot of colour, a lot of people will really take the opportunity to come out and experience the Tour de France – people who've never been to France to watch the race. I expect millions of people will be on the roads."

items.title: Tour de France Femmes 2027 route – The complete stage-by-stage guide
items.author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
items.content:
The 2027 Tour de France Femmes route takes the peloton from Leeds, England, to the summit of the Puy de Dôme in France's Massif Central, over nine days of racing between July 30 and August 7.

There is no rest day, and the race picks up the following day on French soil with a lightly hilly stage 4 to Calais, followed by a punchy stage 5 to Magnanville, where a series of short climbs in the finale will draw the yellow jersey favourites into battle.

Stage 6 into Bourges is a flat track for the sprinters, but stage 7 is anything but, signalling the first of two mountain summit finishes at La Loge des Gardes, which measures 6.7km at an average gradient of 7.1%.

Stage 8 is net downhill and features a descent to the line, but it's another tough stage through the rugged medium mountains of the Massif Central, where the favourites will be exposed against one another.

Finally, the race will come down to a showdown on the Puy de Dôme, the iconic climb of this volcanic region of central France. Measuring 11.3km on irregular gradients averaging 7.8%, it's a huge test that will decide the yellow jersey at the panoramic summit.

Preview the stage-by-stage details below.

Tour de France Femmes 2025 - Stage by stage guide

  • Côte de Kirkheaton, 1.7km at 7.5%
  • Côte de Meltham, 3.2km at 8.4%
  • Côte de Delph, 2.1km at 6.3%

  • Côte de Calton, 1.6km at 6.3%
  • Winnats Pass, 1.4km at 12.3%
  • Côte de Chunal, 1.4km at 7.1%
  • Snake Pass, 5.4km at 4.6%
  • Côte de Bradfield, 1km at 8.8%
  • Côte d'Oughtibridge, 1.5km at 9.1%
  • Côte de Jenkin Road, 0.8kkm at 10.8%

The Tour de France Femmes will feature a first-ever team time trial on an 18km course in the heart of London on the third day of racing.

  • Palace of Westminster, 0.5km
  • St. Paul's Cathedral, 8km
  • Queen Elizabeth Gate, 13km

  • Côte de Harlettes, 1.1km at 6.9%
  • Côte du Ventus, 1.1km at 6.8%
  • Côte de Bazinghen, 0.9km at 7.5%
  • Côte du Cap Blanc, 0.9km at 7.7%

The fifth day will be a more challenging day featuring eight short, punchy climbs on a 161km race from Neufchâtel-en-Bray to Magnanville. Tour organisers classify the stage as 'flat'.

  • Côte d'Osmoy, 1.6km at 5.2%
  • Côte d'Eawy, 1.8km at 4.5%
  • Côte de Molincourt, 1.6km at 4.4%
  • Côte de Dampsmesnil, 1.5km at 6%
  • Côte de Valcorbon, 1.3km at 5.8%
  • Côte de Baudemont, 1km at 10.2%
  • Côte d'Amenucourt, 1km at 10%
  • Côte de Follainville, 1.1km at 6%

Also classified as a flat stage on the sixth day of racing, the peloton will embark on a 138km from Orléans to Bourges. It is a day for pure sprinters, with no categorised climbs on this stage, but it will also offer some reprieve for the overall contenders before the final three days in the mountains.

The peloton will reach the northern foothills of the Massif Central on the seventh day of racing with a hilly 155km from Nevers to La Loge des Gardes. There are only two categorised ascents on tap, both at the very end, which will surely set the stage for the GC battle on the last two days of racing.

  • Côte du Point du Jour, 2.1km at 8.6%
  • La Loge des Gardes, 6.7km at 7.1%

The Tour de France Femmes will visit Clermont-Ferrand for a third time with a 151km route from La Bourboule to Clermont-Ferrand. It is the first official mountain day of racing in the nine-day race, with six categorised climbs and 3,000m of elevation gain.

  • Côte de la Stele, 5.4km at 5%
  • Col de la Croix Saint-Robert, 5.2km at 6.4%
  • Col de la Croix Morand, 6.8km at 5%
  • Côte de Murol, 3.3km at 5.3%
  • Côte de Rouillas, 2.3km at 6.1%
  • Côte de Charade, 6km at 5.9%

The final day of racing will begin in Clermont-Ferrand and take the peloton on a 170km GC battle over eight climbs and 3,800m of elevation gain to the summit of the Puy de Dôme, where the overall winner will be crowned.

  • Côte de Ternant, 5.1km at 6.3%
  • Côte de L'étang des Ouches, 4.7km at 5.1%
  • Côte des Fades, 4.2km at 4.6%
  • Côte du Bouchet, 1.9km at 7%
  • Côte de Boisse, 1.3km at 7.3%
  • Côte de Saint-Jacques-d'Ambur, 2.6km at 5.9%
  • Côte de La Mouteyre, 5.3km at 6.2%
  • Puy de Dôme, 11.3km at 7.8%

items.title: Tour de France 2027 Route Reveal: Brutal Mountains, Big Time Trials, and a Wide-Open Fight for Yellow
items.author: ahood
items.content: Tour de France 2027 packs 71km of time trials, three summit finishes, and a brutal Pyrénées showdown in deceptively challenging course.
items.lbText:
Pogačar will like what he sees in the 2027 Tour de France route. (Photo: Gruber Images)

The 2027 Tour de France is going big on time trials and short on summit finales with its historic return to Great Britain.

Race director Christian Prudhomme unveiled the 114th edition Thursday in Paris, confirming a 3,479km route from Edinburgh to the Champs-Élysées from July 2-25.

The numbers tell the story: 21 stages, 53,450 meters of climbing, six mountain stages but only three summit finales, and two individual time trials totaling 71km, the most since 2012.

Can Remco Evenepoel dare to dream of yellow? Tadej Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard still might have the last word in this deceptively challenging course.

The race opens with three stages across Scotland, England, and Wales before returning to France via Normandy.

Then things get serious. The first week closes with the first of two time trials before driving into the Alps.

Three summit finishes await at Grand Colombier, Les Saisies, and the monstrous Col du Portet in the Pyrénées in the final week.

That’s low by modern standards but these all pack an over-sized bite. There are three other mountain stages that don’t end at a summit but are still loaded with race-breaking climbs.

The Alps also include two ascents of the Côte de Domancy, a preview of the 2027 world championships course in a stage that could explode the GC.

The decisive final week packs in another time trial before the Pyrénées, a brutal Tourmalet and Col du Portet double, and a final mountain showdown to Laruns.

And the favorites? It’s shaping up to be a blockbuster.

Pogačar and Vingegaard will be looking to return to their best after injury setbacks, while rising stars Isaac del Toro and Paul Seixas could elbow in if they race.

The generous time trial distance — the most since Bradley Wiggins won in 2012 — should give Evenepoel favorable terrain, but he will still have to survive the mountain onslaught.

The Tour wraps up July 25 with loops over the dramatic Montmartre climb — yes, it’s back with three passages — before the traditional Champs-Élysées finale.

What’s missing? Iconic climbs like Alpe d’Huez or Mont Ventoux and the race barely touches the Massif Central.

Sprinters will see plenty of chances, with perhaps up to seven sprints, including the penultimate stage that gives the fast men a reason to suffer over the Pyrénées.

With 71km against the clock and a string of monster climbs, the 2027 Tour looks set to reward the complete rider.

Total distance : 3,479km Total elevation gain : 53,450 meters Total stages : 21 Flat stages : 7 Hilly stages : 6 Mountain stages : 6 Individual time trials : 2, totaling 71km, the most since 2012 Summit finishes : 3, at Grand Colombier, Les Saisies, and Saint-Lary-Soulan Col du Portet

items.title: MotoGP "can’t just copy" F1’s Drive to Survive success – Chase Carey
Here is the new Tour de France yellow jersey – Castelli reveals leaders' jerseys for next year's races
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Both races are among the host of events for which the Italian company will provide leaders’ jerseys, the list also including the Vuelta a España, Vuelta Femenina, Paris-Nice and the Tour Auverge-Rhône Alpes.

However, the overall leader’s yellow jersey is the most iconic of all jerseys in our sport and it is the Tour de France which attracts most exposure for Castelli.

"For any cycling apparel brand, producing the Maillot Jaune represents the highest possible honor," said Castelli's Global Brand Manage, Steve Smith. "We wanted these jerseys to be truly special, which is why every micro-detail stems from our deep reverence for what they represent to the sport and the riders who earn them. Beyond pushing performance and aerodynamics, every single feature was crafted to honor that legacy.”

The colours of the jerseys are sacrosanct, and we’ll see no change from recent years, so there’s little room for radical new designs, but Castelli has added some neat little details to each of the jerseys which may make those riders wearing them feel a little more special - if that’s possible.

There’s Tour de France branding on each of the jerseys' zip pulls, which are hexagonal in a nod to France’s nickname, l’Hexagone, and when you open the zip of the yellow jersey, which Castelli say is more vibrant in colour, it reveals a red and blue trim which combines with the white zipper to form France’s flag.

While the red and white Castelli logo is visible on all the jerseys, the chance to incorporate it into the polka-dots of the mountain classification jersey was too good to miss, and adds a touch of class, as do the mountainous profiles on grip strips on the inside hem of the entire range.

The white, young rider’s jersey has undergone the most radical reform, with what they’re calling ultraviolet flashes added to the collar, sleeves and hemline to match the jersey’s new sponsor, Sanofi.

"This is not the first time Castelli and A.S.O. have joined forces around the Tour de France," Smith continued. "We previously produced the leaders' jerseys from 1989 to 1994, worn to historic victories by champions such as Greg LeMond and Miguel Indurain.

"Having supplied leader jerseys during that iconic era, returning to the Tour de France feels like a real homecoming. We are incredibly proud of our heritage in the race, but even more excited to shape its future by outfitting the next generation of champions with garments that push the boundaries of speed, comfort, and style."

Castelli will be providing jersey to a host of other ASO races, and while some, like Paris-Nice will be almost identical to those of the Tour, those of the Vuelta a España and Vuelta Femenina will be different and revealed at a later date.

items.title: Tour de France Femmes 2027 Route Reveal: Savage Puy de Dôme Finale to Decide Everything
items.author: ahood
items.content: Yorkshire hills, a historic London TTT, and a volcanic showdown. The 2027 Tour de France Femmes saves its hardest for last.
items.lbText:
Vollering, shown here celebrating last year, is the early favorite for the 2027 Tour de France Femmes. (Photo: Gruber Images)

The 2027 Tour de France Femmes will break new ground with its first team time trial, a wild opening weekend in Great Britain, and a spectacular final showdown atop the legendary Puy de Dôme.

Race director Marion Rousse unveiled a demanding nine-stage route Thursday in Paris that promises a tight the yellow jersey battle all the way to the final climb.

The sixth edition of the revived women’s Tour starts July 30 in Leeds, England, and finishes August 7 atop the iconic volcano in the heart of central France.

In between, the peloton faces a punishing mix of Yorkshire hills, a historic team time trial through London, opportunities for sprinters and breakaways across northern France, and three decisive stages in the Massif Central.

In total, it’s 1,156km with 17,665m of climbing.

The route saves its biggest fireworks for last, with the Puy de Dôme set to crown the 2027 champion in a spectacular summit showdown.

As already confirmed the 2027 Tour de France Femmes opens with three stages in Great Britain, the race’s third foreign Grand Départ since its revival in 2022, following the Netherlands in 2024 and Switzerland in 2026.

The opening stage takes the peloton from Leeds to Manchester across 85.7km of rolling terrain.

Stage 2 could see an early GC shakeout, with a punishing 154.4km route from Manchester to Sheffield featuring seven categorized climbs and nearly 3,000m of climbing.

The peloton will face a team time trial for the first time since the Femmes revival in 2022.

The 18km course through London on August 1 finishes on The Mall.

After crossing the channel, racing resumes with three transition stages that give something for the sprinters and breakaways as the race hits French tarmac in northern France.

Stage 4 finishes in Calais and stage 5 in Magnanville, with both routes featuring difficult finales that could favor opportunists and puncheurs over the pure sprinters.

The fast finishers should get their best opportunity on stage 6 into Bourges, before the race turns into the gnarled roads of the Massif Central.

Stage 7 finishes atop La Loge des Gardes, the first major summit finale to open a wild final weekend.

The following day, six categorized climbs loom on the road to Clermont-Ferrand across the Massif Central.

The Puy de Dôme, one of the Tour de France’s most storied climbs, will be the battleground for the decisive final stage on August 7.

The twisting volcanic ascent returned to the men’s Tour in 2023 after a 35-year absence, with Michael Woods taking the win.

Now the women’s peloton will race up the legendary steeps overlooking Clermont-Ferrand.

Race organizers hope the battle for yellow to remain undecided until the final kilometer. The brutal slopes of the Puy de Dôme — 14.2km at 7.6% — could produce a dramatic, final-day reversal.

Who’s the course favor? On paper, defending champion Demi Vollering, as she targets a historic third Tour de France Femmes crown.

The Dutch star, who also won the 2026 world road title, can do it all on the punchy terrain and steep climbs of the Massif Central.

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, who joins Lidl-Trek for 2027, will be among her principal rivals, along with Pauline Ferrand-Prévot and Marlen Reusser.

Emerging star Paula Blasi, who joins Movistar, could also be a major contender after her fifth-place debut in 2026.

What’s missing? The course avoids both the Alps and the Pyrénées and the longer, sustained climbs that favor the pure climbers like Ferrand-Prévot and Niewiadoma.

items.title: 'Not what a captain should be' - the debate around Fernandes' outburst
items.content: <article>Bruno Fernandes' comments after Manchester United's humbling by Como have got fans and pundits talking - but what now for the captain?</article>
items.lbText:
Bruno Fernandes' comments after Manchester United's humbling by Como have got fans and pundits talking - but what now for the captain?

United's 4-1 Champions League defeat in Italy was the result of a wretched performance and Fernandes questioned boss Michael Carrick's tactics.

"It's a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence," said the Portugal attacking midfielder on TNT Sports.

Asked if Carrick got his tactics wrong, the 32-year-old continued: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me."

Fernandes rounds on Carrick after Man Utd humiliation

Man Utd humbling by Como leaves Carrick job in danger

Not according to former Liverpool vice-captain Jamie Carragher, working as a summariser, on CBS Sports.

"He's reacted like that because he's been embarrassed by the manager [who] brought him off," said the ex-England defender.

"And when he talks about pressing, whether it's man-to-man or zonal, for years, Bruno Fernandes has meant Manchester United can't press because he does things for the crowd.

"He runs all over the place like a kid in the schoolyard for the supporters. They all think he's working hard. He's not. He's killing the rest of the team doing it."

He added: "Watching him throw his arms up every week in a game is an absolute disgrace [and] calling the manager out considering how he's performed this season on the pitch.

"[It's an] awful attitude and not what a Manchester United captain should be."

Fernandes' comments come a week after defender Lisandro Martinez made similar headlines following United's previous Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid.

The Argentine said he expected more investment in the squad and "more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]". He later apologised.

And while Martinez's outburst sparked debate, Fernandes' comments could have even larger repercussions.

Carrick, who was under huge pressure already following a terrible start to the season, said in reply: "There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."

United have not won in their past seven games since beating Champions League minnows Sabah. They have just one win in their seven Premier League games this season.

Not many people have defended Fernandes' public questioning of the tactics.

But some do understand his frustrations.

Former Leicester and Celtic keeper Kasper Schmeichel, whose dad Peter won the Champions League, five Premier League titles and three FA Cups as a United player, said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "Given last week and what's happened, he probably should not be saying these things because it's only going to add to the problems.

"With experience you learn that you need to keep these things in-house. It's a problem, with everything that happened during the week.

"Michael Carrick didn't need this, the club didn't need this. It's exposing all of the issues that are at Manchester United.

"It's very plain to see that there are loads of issues but you need to be fixing them, you need to be having meetings within the club, which I'm sure that they are, but it's obviously not resolved. It's just translating on to the pitch."

The issue that most pundits have is not that Fernandes has these opinions - but that he has let the world know them.

Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock, speaking on BBC Match of the Day, said: "I think there will be ex-players now from Manchester United saying, 'why are you letting this get out, this should be a collective in the changing room where we come together'.

"Whether you like the manager or not, you've got to come together and say 'OK how do we correct this?'

"Senior players go to the manager and say 'listen we didn't agree with the tactics, we didn't think we got it right, how do we go about this, how do we move forward', because you start airing it in public and it doesn't end well for anyone."

Former Chelsea midfielder Joe Cole on TNT Sports called it "sacrilege".

"I've played for managers where I don't agree with the tactics but you might say that to your mate or to your wife. You don't come out as captain of the club and question the manager," he said.

Andy Mitten, editor of United We Stand, told BBC 5 Live Breakfast that Fernandes has "thrown his coach under the bus".

"And Manchester United fans are divided as to whether he should or should not do that. Last week, Martinez was also critical. A lot of Manchester United fans agreed with him.

"Again, there's mitigation, he wants a new contract. That's because he's not been playing enough, because he's been injured. And injuries are a real problem for Manchester United. There's no recognised centre-forward. So it is a really difficult time for United."

Former United midfielder Carrick, who took over in January initially as caretaker manager, seemed to blank his players at full-time before heading over to the United fans.

"I don't blame him for ignoring the players," said Mitten.

"He went to the fans and he held his hands up and he said, 'I'm sorry'.

"You can tell he's hurting. He's a Manchester United fan himself. He was a season ticket holder only a year ago before he took the job. I think he's trying his best, but it's just not working at the moment. Manchester United are really, really struggling."

Fernandes has been Manchester United's one consistent outstanding player since a £47m move from Sporting in January 2020, when Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was the manager.

He has scored 111 goals and made 106 assists in 338 games for the club in all competitions.

Former manager Erik ten Hag made him the skipper in the summer of 2023 after taking the armband off Harry Maguire, whose place in the team was far from certain.…

items.title: Cannondale’s Connecticut HQ to close with the global headquarters moving to the Netherlands
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
American bike brand Cannondale is set to close down its Connecticut headquarters as part of a restructuring by its parent company, Pon Holdings and its US brands; the move is set to see multiple jobs lost.

For years, the company’s global headquarters has been in Wilton, Connecticut, but operations there will be wound down over the next eight months, with the company’s global base moving to Woudenberg, Netherlands, which currently serves as the European HQ.

Research and development, which is currently based in Freiburg, Germany, will continue.

The company’s North American HQ will consolidate with Pon’s other bike brands, Cervélo and Santa Cruz, moving to the West Coast. While it’s said each brand will retain its own identity, Pon says the move will "strengthen its North American operations and retailer support."

"This builds on two years of closer commercial collaboration between the brands to offer retailers greater choice.

"For retailers carrying more than one brand, this means a single point of contact and simpler ordering and support services.

"The aim is to make it easier for retailers to work with Cannondale and access more of the Pon. Bike portfolio," the company’s press release said.

Cannondale has been on the US bike scene since opening for business in Wilton, Connecticut, in 1971, and has established itself as one of the world’s largest bike manufacturers. Dutch multinational Pon Holdings acquired the brand from Dorel Sports in 2021.

The developments come just months after it was announced that Cannondale’s Dutch factory would close, with production moving to Lithuania and Germany and that their Mountain bike team, Cannondale Factory Racing, would close at the end of the year.

Despite its scale, the brand has always had a left-field feel, with its race winning, single-sided Lefty front suspension fork perhaps the company's most radical design. On the road, the brand currently supplies bikes to the EF Education-EasyPost WorldTour and EF Education-Oatly Women’s WorldTour teams.

"The entire office will be closed and almost all employees there will be impacted," said Cannondale’s Global VP, People, Maggie Lansdale, according to PinkBike.

"The first separations are expected to occur on December 21, 2026, and separations are expected to continue in phases through December 31, 2027. The closure and separations will be permanent."

items.title: Tour de France 2027 route unveiled with British start, 71km of time trials, and a brutal queen stage as highlights
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
The route for the 2027 Tour de France has been unveiled, with a testing British Grand Départ, two individual time trials, and a brutal Pyrenean queen stage among the highlight obstacles that reigning champion Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) and his challengers will have to face come July.

Race Director Christian Prudhomme revealed the route on Thursday at the Palais de Congrès in Paris, with the most ITT kilometres since 2012, when Bradley Wiggins took victory, totalling 71km across two key days against the clock.

Action kicks off from the Scottish capital, Edinburgh, on Friday, July 2, and 21 stages over 3,479km will stand in the way of whether or not Pogačar can win his fourth yellow jersey in a row and a record-breaking sixth overall crown in Paris.

The Pyrenees are set to star as the defining mountain range of the 114th Tour, arriving in the final week with a brutal duo of stages, including the hardest day on paper to the Col du Portet on stage 18, but the Alps and Massif Central will still play a major role in the race for the maillot jaune.

Even nine months ahead of the Scottish start, Pogačar is the benchmark that two-time Tour winner Jonas Vingegaard (Visma-Lease a Bike), this year's runner-up Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), and rising French superstar Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM) will all be chasing.

If he is to take a sixth overall victory, the Slovenian would move him ahead of Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault, and Miguel Induráin for the all-time record of titles.

After likely battling out the race for the first yellow jersey on stage 1 in Carlisle, there are six probably flat stages in total where the sprinters and lead-out trains will want to come to the fore, with plenty on offer also for the rouleurs and Classics specialists as the race traverses south from the UK.

There would have been seven clear chances for the fast men, but the drama-producing Butte Montmartre climb has returned for a third year in a row in 2027 on the final day, making the run to the Champs-Élysées anything but a guarantee for those eyeing a sprint on stage 21 in Paris.

Organisers ASO want the GC race to be on for as long as possible, with a crescendo building towards the most difficult day on stage 18, where a back-loaded route will all but reach its denouement atop the Col du Portet summit finish, if someone isn't already out of sight.

Twenty years after the Tour started in London, and 13 years after mass crowds delighted the Tour in Yorkshire, the start in Great Britain is characterised by an opening flatter day, and two hilly stages to Liverpool and Cardiff, the second of which should bring the first major GC action.

in the tricky Welsh hills has five punchy climbs packed into the last 80km of a 223km day. The GC hopefuls will have to be at their best while the Classics specialists – including Pogačar – will surely be on all-out attack.

With more than 3,000m of elevation gain, it is a likely place for a signature Pogačar attack ahead of the first rest day, which is more of a travel day down to Normandy from the UK's south coast.

The first of two individual time trials comes on stage 7, where four-time ITT World Champion Evenepoel will be expected to take control over a flat 38km race against the clock in Chambord. The tension will be building over punchy finishes into the first few stages in France ahead of this important test.

Evenepoel has already won three time trials at the Tour, but without a major mountain stage in the first week, this could bring the Belgian his first stint in the yellow jersey, 51 years after the last Belgian winner of the Tour, Lucien Van Impe, unless Pogačar launched an early campaign of destruction on stages like the one to Cardiff.

If not, then he will have been keeping his powder dry for the Jura and the first trip up to the high mountains on stage 9, where a climb he has won before rears its head again: .

Pogačar took the second of his 26 Tour stage wins on the Grand Colombier on stage 15 of the 2020 race before winning his first yellow jersey, and now the 17.4-kilometre climb and its 7.1% average gradient represent the first opportunity to land a blow against your GC rivals. It arrives via the Col du Berthiand (6.3km at 7.5%), Côte de Neyrolles (3.6 at 7.7%), and Col de Richemond (7.7km at 6%), as the first of three mountain stages in a row.

As racing resumes after the first true rest day in Haute-Savoie, the host of the World Championships in 2027 will get a dress rehearsal for the rainbow jersey race on stage 10, a brutally difficult 171km route from Annecy to Sallanches.

The key climb of Worlds road races, the Côte de Domancy, will feature on the route as one of six tough climbs in the Alps. It's an ascent Vingegaard knows and loves, having demolished Pogačar there at the 2023 Tour en route to a second overall title.

But as we know, the Slovenian often likes to take revenge on the climbs where he has been burned in the past, and after missing out on defending his rainbow jersey this September, he will be hungry to make a statement.

The Tour will depart the Alps after just one more day of racing there, but it doesn't waste that opportunity, with the second hardest day on paper arriving on stage 11 to Les Saisies.

  • Time trials
    • Mountain stages
      • Summit finishes
        • Stage 9 to Grand Colombier
        • Stage 18 to Col du Portet

      More than 4,700m of elevation gain across four massive climbs feature, heading onto the Col de la Colombière (15.9km at 7%) straight out of neutral, and never really dropping in difficulty as it passes over the Col de la Croix Fry (7.2km at 5.5%), Col de la Forclaz de Queige (5.1km at 8.2%), Col du Pré (12.6km at 7.8%), and Montée de Bisanne (12.4km at 8.3%), before the final push to Les Saisies.

      After that complete reshuffle of the GC standings, the race settles into two sprint stages, but there won't be overly long for the riders to catch their breath, as they then reach the Massif Central, where 4,300 metres of elevation gain are tucked into a quite tough day to Mende on stage 14.

      The last time Mende appeared as a stage finish in 2022, there weren't major gaps between the GC favourites, as Michael Matthews won from the breakaway, but the approach to the finish in 2027 is over tougher terrain and steeper climbs, making the viciously steep Côte de la Croix Neuve (3km at 10.1%) more threatening than before.

      One of the big favourites will likely be in control by the time the second week reaches a close, but there can be no room for complacency heading into the final six-stage run towards Paris, with plenty of opportunities to lose and gain major time.

      The second individual time trial on stage 16 kicks this off, bringing the total kilometres against the clock to 71, returning the Tour to a stage closer to that of the Team Sky years, where Wiggins, Chris Froome and Geraint Thomas utilised the ITTs to their advantage, sometimes against the stronger climbers.

      This lands massively in favour of 2026 runner-up Evenepoel, who will likely have already won stage 7 and be looking to double up and further his chances of a repeat podium, or even higher. Staying with Pogačar atop Grand Colombier and in the Alps is far from a given, though, so for Evenepoel to even be within striking distance before stage 16 in Toulouse will be a tall order.

      What the 33km stage could do is potentially close the gap down before the Pyrenees, and this stage should also work in favour of home star Seixas, but Pogačar and Vingegaard are still not to be sniffed at – especially this far into a Grand Tour.

      What's certain is that the hardest stage of the race will come on stage 18: 174km, 5,400m of elevation gain, and four of the hardest climbs in the race and France packed into one day of Pyrenean fireworks, set to really separate the wheat from the chaff at the 144th Tour.

      Pogačar once again will return to favourable ground on a climb he has previously conquered, the Col du Portet (16km at 8.7%), which will serve as the summit finish and the Souvenir Henri Desgrange – the prize honouring the former director at the highest peak of the race.

      To get there, the GC favourites will have to survive the Col du Soulor (11.8km at 7.3%), Col du Tourmalet (19km at 7.4%), and Hourquette d'Ancizan (8.2km at 5.1%), with the Tourmalet's iconic slopes arriving with 70km still to go and offering up the chance for more daring, long range raids.

      Portet hasn't been seen in the Tour since 2021, when Pogačar defeated Vingegaard and Richard Carapaz en route to a dominant second yellow jersey title, but it will now headline the 2027 edition, as the likely penultimate major GC day.

      If yellow isn't all but decided by this point, which would be a major shock, then a second day in the Pyrenees will become the decider on stage 19, from Hasparren to Laruns, where the final climb to the Col de Marie Blanque (7.7km at 8.6%) presents the final chance for a long-range move, cresting 19km from the downhill run to the line.

      For now, Pogačar looks the most likely to be in yellow again at this point, but who knows what eight more months of development for Seixas and Evenepoel could look like – and Vingegaard isn't to be counted out with such brutal stages either.

      In theory, there could be a final day for major GC splits on the final day into Paris, with the triple ascent of the Côte de la Butte Montmartre again punctuating the final day, but GC times actually being taken and not neutralised as they have been the past two years looks unlikely.

      The Tour isn't just for climbers, even if yellow is the main prize, with plenty on offer over 12 potential non-GC days.

      With many of the best and most popular riders in the world being puncheurs or Classics specialists, it is in ASO's best interest to have days that suit the likes of Mathieu van der Poel (Alpecin-Premier Tech), Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike), and Mads Pedersen (Lidl-Trek) on the route.

      They've got them in abundance in 2027, especially in the first week, with stage 2 to Liverpool and stage 3 to Cardiff resembling profiles of Classics, with up-and-down tight roads in the UK set to bring the most explosive riders to the fore.

      Van der Poel and Van Aert have lit up hilly finishes in recent years, as have Pogačar and his newest lieutenant Isaac del Toro, so the GC riders likely won't be counted out of any of the short but steep uphill finales, such as on stage 4 to Cherbourg-en-Cotentin, the first day in France, or the following stage to Plumelec.

      • Punchy uphill finishes
        • Stage 4 to Cherbourg-en-Cotentin
      • Classics-style stages:
        • Sprint stages

          Stage 8 to Le Creusot also brings the same riders into play, but also represents a great opportunity for the breakaway, ahead of the first mountain stage. It's also the longest stage of the 2027 edition, with two tough climbs – the Col de la Croix de la Libération (4.6km at 5.3%) and Signal d'Uchon (5.7km at 5.7%) – preceding the uphill run to the line.

          Rodez to Albi at the close of the second week on stage 15 represents the likely final chance for the explosive Classics riders, until the last day in Paris, where Van der Poel's inspired win from a breakaway with Pogačar – just surviving ahead of the sprinters – should serve as inspiration for anyone with any punch left to get on the attack.

          At least six of the 12 non-GC days should be for the sprinters, including the opening day from Edinburgh to Carlisle, and flat finishes into Angers, Valence, Montpellier, Pau, and Libourne, with stage 21 to Paris also potentially going the way of the fast men depending on how it is raced.

          While the race for yellow has mostly been a dictatorship – or at most a duopoly if you go back from 2020 onwards – in recent years, sprinting has been more of a democracy, with the likes of Tim Merlier (Soudal-QuickStep), Jasper Philipsen (Alpecin-Premier Tech), Jonathan Milan (Lidl-Trek), and Biniam Girmay (NSN) among those sharing the spoils in recent seasons.

          Merlier stands above as the best for the moment, but that balance of power changes quickly. However, all of the quick men will be thinking most about how they navigate the road from Edinburgh down to Carlisle, with a rare shot at yellow.
